#265. Better educated than ever — yet Germany's Gen Z is being shut out of its own future

Never before have young people around the world been so well-educated while facing so many economic challenges. Young Germans are asking: Will I be better off than my parents?

It is becoming increasingly difficult for young people in Germany to find a job after finishing university or professional training. And finding an affordable place to live in a big city, and finally starting to live independently is becoming almost impossible.

Furthermore, young people do not feel that politicians are taking action on issues that matter to them, such as climate protection. The climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, is a case in point. It, therefore, shouldn't be a surprise that young people across Europe once again took to the streets this Friday, which was World Children's Day too, to make their voices heard. In Germany, Gen Z protests took place in 73 towns and cities.

What particularly infuriates many young people is being talked about rather than spoken to. Equally infuriating is seeing their protests branded as criminal before they have even begun, all because of the actions of a small minority.

One example of such rhetoric was when the youth wing of the conservative Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) party in Berlin-Mitte suggested deploying the German army against demonstrations.

It can also be seen in the media, such as when Bild, Germany's highest-circulation tabloid, ran a headline that translated as: "Young, male, known to the police — who rioted after the demonstrations and where chaos threatens today."

"Young people are taking to the streets because they feel they are not being heard. And, of course, that feeling is strongly reinforced when the press devotes no more than a brief paragraph to their demands while focusing the rest of its coverage on how these protests could become problematic," says Erik Sczygiol, who until recently was deputy secretary-general of the Federal Conference of Student Representatives. "Of course, any potential security concerns need to be addressed, but they should not overshadow media coverage of the protests."

The 18-year-old Sczygiol is almost an exception. He was invited to participate in the launch of the World Population Report in Bonn alongside representatives of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and the German Foundation for World Population (DSW). This year's report, entitled "Succeeding Generations: Empowering young people to chart the future," is particularly noteworthy because it focuses on Gen Z.

UN researchers surveyed 109,000 people across 73 countries for the report, some of whose findings are encouraging. Young people worldwide are better educated than any generation before them, with 78% of adolescents across the globe completing at least lower secondary education. But finding a job is becoming increasingly difficult, while informal employment is on the rise.

This economic uncertainty has far-reaching consequences for young people. According to the report, people often do not achieve financial independence until they are in their mid-to-late 20s, and a stable partnership and parenthood are often not realities before their early-to-mid 30s.

Nor do young people have a seat at the political decision-making table when it comes to shaping future reforms in the labor market, housing or climate protection. Florian Brod, 25, points out: "Almost half of the world's population is under 30, yet only 2.6% of parliamentarians worldwide are under 30."

Young people need and want change to protect their livelihoods and those of future generations. "Yet those who will have to live longest with the consequences of today's decisions are precisely the ones who have hardly any representation in the political decision-making process," says Brod.

He is somewhat close to the political decision-making process as he has served as a Youth Delegate for Sustainable Development for almost two years. In this role, he represents the interests of young people in Germany at United Nations conferences. This is certainly an important step towards giving his generation a greater say in political processes.

Nevertheless, both Brod and Sczygiol have had similar experiences. They often participate in conferences and panel discussions and are invited to submit their opinions, but these invitations often amount to little more than symbolic gestures.

"Having access to an international conference is a first step. But without substantive briefings ahead of the conference, without involvement in preliminary negotiations and, in some cases, without access to negotiation texts, there is little opportunity for us to help shape the outcome. When young people see their demands making little headway politically while they are simultaneously excluded from the search for solutions, frustration inevitably builds," says Brod.

Sczygiol adds: "We often get the feeling at the Federal Youth Conference that we were invited simply to provide a nice photo opportunity. We may be sitting at the table, but often only once a bill has already gone through 17 different drafts and is just days away from its final vote in the Bundestag. By that stage, young people have virtually no say in changing anything, and their voices are barely heard. Their contributions are often simply dismissed with: 'Well, that's just typical youthful nonsense.' And that is something that really frustrates young people."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Medical student Amelie Belosevic knows that feeling all too well. She served as Germany's Youth Delegate at the World Health Assembly in Geneva in May. Twenty-five countries sent youth representatives, which Belosevic sees as a clear step forward. However, she has one criticism. According to the United Nations Population Fund, 90% of the world's 1.8 billion young people live in the Global South. Yet, the region was represented by only eight delegates. As a result, Africa, Latin America and large parts of Asia were left virtually voiceless.

Her demands for Germany include better job prospects for young people entering the workforce and sustainable pension systems 40 years from now. "For a very long time, people have said 'I believe my children will have a better life than I do.' But that is no longer necessarily true. So it makes sense then that those who feel the greatest anxiety about the future are the people who have most of their life ahead of them. Sometimes, people don't understand that. We young people need to be able to believe in our future again!"

Muse in Instagram will still be more limited than the actual Muse app or web interface, though. While you can send it to-dos or have it track Instagram-specific tasks, you'll probably still need to use the Muse app or website to see what it does with all your Instagram messages.

#261. Has the 'Parthenon puzzle' been solved? The long quest to reassemble lost eastern pediment

The depiction of the birth of the goddess Athena above the Parthenon's entrance is considered a masterpiece of ancient art. Now, a German research team has pieced together all the surviving fragments.

The 2,500-year-old Parthenon is ancient Greece's most important temple and is regarded as one of the greatest masterpieces of the High Classical period of Greek art.

Dedicated to Athena, the city's patron goddess, it towers over Athens from its position on the Acropolis — a powerful symbol of the city's importance.

The Parthenon had a lasting influence on Western ideas of humanity and art. The sculptures adorning its pediments, created under the direction of the legendary sculptor Phidias, are considered unparalleled examples of proportion and grace. They have influenced artists from ancient Rome through Neoclassicism to the modern era.

The east pediment above the temple entrance depicted the birth of the goddess Athena from the head of her father Zeus, surrounded by the Olympian gods. A total of 39 figures adorned the roughly 29-meter-long work of art. At its center stood a colossal Zeus figure, measuring 3.8 meters in height.

For centuries, scholars have puzzled over exactly what the arrangement looked like, as the pediment was destroyed during the Christianization of Greece.

After decades of painstaking detective work and with the help of modern technology, archaeologist Vinzenz Brinkmann and his team have managed to piece together all the surviving fragments of the Parthenon's east pediment.

Brinkmann heads the Antiquities and Asia department at Frankfurt's Liebieghaus sculpture collection. "We're very, very confident that we've solved the mystery," he told DW.

The results are now on display in an exhibition at the Liebieghaus titled "Athena, the Stage is Yours: The Parthenon Puzzle."

Only around 20% of the original marble sculpture's volume is known to have survived. The fragments are scattered across various European museums, with most located in Athens. The British Museum also holds numerous pieces.

Brinkmann and his wife, Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, have spent more than 40 years working on this ancient puzzle, with so many of its pieces missing.

And they were far from the first to attempt it: "Already in the 19th century, many scholars studied the subject and developed well-founded theories based on their deep knowledge of ancient sources," Brinkmann explains.

In 1910, a study documenting the many fragments held by the British Museum was published. The research team was able to build on that earlier work, but progress remained slow for years.

Then, in 2014, a visit to the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg provided Brinkmann with a crucial clue. There, he encountered a Roman sarcophagus featuring a relief of Athena's birth. "That's when it suddenly clicked: They're all there!"

Nine such sarcophagi are known to exist, almost all of them in Rome. Each depicts a different section of the Parthenon's east pediment.

Brinkmann emphasizes that other scholars had already noticed this connection in the 19th century. "But we really seized on the idea and never let go."

The researchers also benefited from 21st-century technology: 3D scanners and printers. Brinkmann and his team visited numerous destinations to examine around 60 original fragments at different locations — traveling light. An iPhone was all they needed to scan the pieces.

Digitally fitting the fragments together led to another important discovery. "We know these figures we're putting together!" Brinkmann recalls thinking at the time.

The Romans had repeatedly made individual copies of all the sculptures from the pediment. "These copies matched the fragments perfectly. Suddenly, we found ourselves surrounded by old acquaintances we had never suspected had come from the pediment." This finally enabled the researchers to reconstruct all the figures and their original arrangement.

Using a 3D printer, the team created a 4-meter-long model at a scale of 1:7.7. For the exhibition, they also produced life-size 3D prints of the most important fragments and mounted them on panels depicting the complete figures at their original size. An animation brings the reconstructed composition to life, digitally assembling the fragments to reveal how the east pediment once looked.

Alongside works from the Liebieghaus collection, the exhibition features loans from other institutions, including the Vatican Museums and the Louvre. Objects from the Acropolis Museum in Athens had originally been expected as well. But Greece withdrew its participation after learning that the British Museum was also planning to lend fragments to the Frankfurt exhibition. The Liebieghaus ultimately decided to forgo the British-owned fragments, too.

There is a reason for this controversy. Britain holds a substantial portion of the Parthenon frieze as well as fragments from both pediments.

Greek authorities have been campaigning for their return for decades.

In Britain, the 56 sections of the frieze are known as the "Elgin Marbles," named after Lord Elgin, the British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire in Constantinople.

In the early 19th century, Elgin had sculptures removed from the exterior of the Parthenon on the Acropolis in Athens. They were taken to Britain with the consent of the Ottoman Empire, which ruled Greece at the time.

Britain maintains that the sculptures were legally acquired.

For years, the dispute remained deadlocked. Since the Labour Party came to power in Britain, there has been some movement toward resolving it. But apparently not enough to persuade Greece to lend artworks to an exhibition in which the British Museum might also participate.

The exhibition "Athena, the Stage is Yours. The Parthenon Puzzle" runs through July 25, 2027, at the Liebieghaus in Frankfurt.

This article was originally written in German.

#260. Why your MacBook desktop Spaces keep rearranging themselves and how to stop it

Disable a Mission Control-specific setting to keep Spaces from switching.

In macOS, Spaces are virtual desktops that help organize and manage open apps and windows. macOS allows up to 16 dedicated spaces for organizing your desktop. While fullscreen and split-mode apps also function like Spaces, they are different from numbered Spaces, particularly in how you access them using keyboard shortcuts.You can dedicate specific tasks to individual Spaces, such as communication, media consumption and web browsing. Another benefit to using Spaces is that they help consolidate open windows and prevent them from moving between virtual desktops when you switch Spaces.

While Spaces are particularly useful in organizing your desktop experience, their shortcomings become apparent when you notice their order changing in Mission Control as you switch between them. This happens when you use the command + tab shortcut to switch Spaces, and macOS rearranges them depending on which Space was recently accessed. If you prefer having Spaces in an order of your choosing, the default auto-rearrangement feature can become frustrating.

However, the good news is that you don't have to be stuck with this feature forever. There's an option tucked away inside macOS' Settings app that prevents Spaces from rearranging themselves. Disabling it is all you need to make Spaces behave consistently on your MacBook or other macOS devices.

Specifically, a toggle relevant to Mission Control is what causes Spaces to rearrange themselves on macOS, and it's enabled by default. To disable it, click the Apple icon in the menu bar and then click System Settings to open the Settings app. You can also use Spotlight search to look for System Settings.

While in the Settings app, click Desktop & Dock to bring up options specific to customizing your desktop experience. Scroll all the way to the bottom of these options to find the Mission Control section. Now, look for Automatically rearrange Spaces based on most recent use and disable it to stop Spaces from rearranging themselves.

That's it! You can now freely arrange and move between your Spaces without having to worry about macOS messing with them. Your Mac offers three options to navigate Spaces, including the three or four-finger trackpad swipe, Control + left/right arrow key shortcut and using the pointer to choose from available Spaces in Mission Control.

macOS offers several useful tools that, when combined, can help you get the most out of Spaces. For example, even though you cannot officially rename Spaces, they can still be assigned individual wallpapers for visual identity. You can do this by disabling the toggle to Show on all Spaces when changing wallpapers in a desktop Space.

Similarly, you can enable additional shortcuts besides those that let you switch between Spaces for a more control and precision. You can access these shortcuts from Settings > Keyboard Shortcuts > Mission Control > Mission Control drop-down menu. You'll see a list of shortcuts depending on the number of available Spaces, and you can enable individual shortcuts based on your requirements.

Additionally, you can incorporate Hot Corners in your workflow for a more robust multitasking experience. Hot Corners allow you to assign specific functions to the four corners of your display, including an option to launch Mission Control. Since Spaces are inherently tied to Mission Control, the ability to flick the pointer to a corner and view all active Spaces at a glance can save valuable time.

Likewise, at times you might want to access an app from any Space, for example, Apple Music, to make music control simpler and more accessible. In such cases, Control + click the app in the dock > options > assign to All Desktop to make the chosen app persist across Spaces.

#258. No more heated seat subscriptions for cars in New York from 2027

Services with “ongoing costs” are a pretty big loophole in the new law.

Car buyers in New York may find the cost of ownership reduces a little next year. Maybe. Governor Kathy Hochul signed a bill yesterday that bans car companies and dealerships from locking up car features behind a subscription, a law that goes into effect on February 27 next year.

“People spending their hard-earned money on a car shouldn’t have to fork over even more money for features that should automatically come with the car. My message to car companies is clear: this kind of deceptive business model isn’t going to fly in New York State. Keep your hands out of New Yorkers’ wallets,” the governor said.

In the old days, the only options you paid to use after you bought a car were mods or upgrades you installed after the fact. That started to change with services like General Motors’ OnStar, which introduced telematics to the vehicle—for a monthly fee.

We end users might not like having to open our wallets each month, but the capital markets sure do, and car companies love making the capital markets happy. Which is why there has been such a push toward connected vehicles. Remote start and predictive maintenance alerts are nice, but your regular payments to the car company—plus any data of yours it can sell—is the goal.

Some automakers have gone even further. Infamously, BMW and its heated seats. Like the McDonald’s coffee lawsuit, it’s a fact half-remembered; BMW North America never tried such a thing, just in countries like South Korea and the UK, and in 2023 BMW’s board said that subscriptions would only be for software-related features from then on.

New York’s press release mentions heated seats but also calls out a number of other modern tech features: “enhanced navigation, hands-free driving and entertainment options that do not present an ongoing expense for dealers and manufacturers.”

But the way the actual law is written appears to leave a rather large loophole, at least to these eyes.

S.9348A/A.10411A prohibits motor vehicle manufacturers, dealers or third-party service providers from adding subscription services or charging post-purchase fees for any motor vehicle feature that uses pre-installed components or hardware that do not have an ongoing cost. As vehicles become more advanced, the new law aims to establish clear rules preventing exploitative practices and prevent post-purchase fees as a future automotive business model.

A heated seat might not have “an ongoing cost,” but the maps and databases that enable “enhanced navigation” and “hands-free driving” systems definitely do, as these need to be constantly updated. A regular cadence of software updates also generates an ongoing cost to an OEM, arguably. And car companies pay for plenty of lawyers who really love to argue.

And so, while experiments like BMW’s seat heater subscription won’t be allowed in the state, the new rule might still allow for plenty of ongoing fees for services like OnStar or Mercedes’ Drive Assist Pro system we tested recently.

#257. COP31: No agreement on climate science, disinformation spreading

Attacks on climate science and disinformation risk delaying key measures at COP31 in Antalya. As the UN climate talks draw to a close, how will that affect efforts to come to an agreement?

The annual UN climate conference is the place where countries negotiate the world's plans to limit global warming and adapt to its consequences — and who will pay for climate action as well as damage from storms, floods and droughts.

But this year at COP31 in Antalya, an ongoing dispute over the timing of a key assessment of global warming is risking the scientific foundations of global climate action, say observers.

"We are extremely concerned about the situation," said a diplomat with the European delegation who could not speak on the record, adding that it came down to the future of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the world's leading body of climate scientists.

The IPCC's scientific assessments, published every six to seven years, provide the basis for major international climate agreements, including the 2015 Paris Agreement. The IPCC began evaluating the latest climate science in 1988 and its most recent report was published in 2023.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Researchers should have actually already started work on the next edition but the last plenary session was put on hold in October at the urging of Russia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and Kenya.

"The IPCC finds itself in a difficult situation," a spokesperson from the German Environment Ministry told DW at COP. "We stand ready to help resolve this issue, so that the panel can continue its work. To that end, we are holding many discussions with various countries to explore possible solutions."

At the core of the dispute is the question of whether future UN climate talks base their negotiations on the latest scientific knowledge — or not.

That's especially relevant for the next "global stocktake," due in 2028, a report card on the world's climate efforts, which will shape action plans for countries around the world to lower planet-heating greenhouse gas emissions.

The European Union, Brazil, the United Kingdom, small island states and several other countries especially at risk of the effects of climate change have called for the IPCC's seventh assessment report to be published in 2028, so it can be used to inform next steps for climate action. The report covers climate protection and impact.

"It's much more difficult without these scientific reports. Otherwise, we're just talking to ourselves or relying on information that's no longer current," said a delegation source.

But Russia, Iran, India and Saudi Arabia want the IPCC report postponed until 2029, after the global stocktake.

The official reason: the tight timeline would be detrimental to the quality of the research, and could hinder the participation of researchers and governments representing developing countries.

Disagreements over budget issues have also held up the IPCC's work. Among other expenses, the funds are used to pay the travel arrangements for the hundreds of volunteer scientists, especially those from poorer countries, to attend the IPCC sessions.

"No budget means no more IPCC," said a member from another delegation, also speaking on condition of anonymity.

It hasn't come to that point yet, but without planning certainty the whole process risks being delayed — along with the climate negotiations that depend on this knowledge.

Researchers with the IPCC, however, have said the timeline is attainable.

"We have no time to lose," said an open letter released in October signed by more than 100 researchers from 36 countries — including India and China. "We stand committed to continue working to deliver the [seventh assessment report] in a manner that is rigorous, timely and inclusive."

But while the dispute over the timeline won't alter the scientific findings themselves, it could delay their political impact.

In its pre-COP communications, France accused the countries delaying the report's publication schedule of attempting to "obstruct science in order to lower the ambition of the global stocktake."

The IPCC isn't a stranger to attempts at political persuasion: At past climate conferences, delegates from many countries have regularly negotiated the exact phrasing of the summary reports intended for policymakers.

Speaking at COP31 on November 17, EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said it was "fundamental to protect the integrity of climate science and the role of the IPCC as the source of best available science."

Although there is no vote on the IPCC at COP31, it's possible that its significance and a timeline for the next report will be included in the final declaration of the climate talks, expected this weekend.

The IPCC has been warning for years that disinformation is hindering global climate action. And the struggle for information and control over the narrative in Antalya hasn't just been limited to the IPCC.

This was apparent in a document DW obtained that had been sent anonymously to several less wealthy countries' delegations in the run-up to COP31.

It claimed to explain the nature of Turkey's proposed goals for boosting electrification to 35% by 2035, but went on to misrepresent several core details of the plans to make them seem less appealing to developing countries than they are in reality.

At least two countries confirmed to DW that they had received the document. It did not state where it hailed from and was labeled as an "equity assessment."

The presentation portrays electrification as a business venture undertaken by wealthy countries at the expense of poorer nations. The International Energy Agency, however, has calculated that developing countries could save around $100 billion (€90 billion) in fossil fuel imports by 2035 through electrification.

The presentation also gives the impression that all countries must meet fixed electrification targets. In fact, according to the UN, the 35% target represents a global goal, with individual countries free to determine their own national pathways.

This article was originally written in German.

#256. How much does it cost to replace an out-of-warranty Tesla battery?

A Tesla battery can last for years beyond its warranty, but replacing it once that coverage runs out could cost you more than $20,000.

Being a Tesla owner sure makes you look cool and environmentally friendly, especially compared to your neighbor's gas-guzzling car. But all that excitement starts to fade when the EV doesn't go the distance it used to and a battery replacement feels like it's in the cards. Running a Tesla with an expired warranty can be nerve-racking, especially because a battery replacement could cost anywhere from about $12,600 to more than $20,000.

How much you end up paying depends on your car's model and what other parts need repairing or swapping, but Tesla gives you no pricing chart to prepare for the expensive journey ahead. The thing is, battery degradation is just basic chemistry, so losing a few miles of range as that EV gets older should not surprise you, even if you avoid the leading causes of EV battery damage. It isn't exactly a sign for you to worry about a full battery replacement either.

A 2025 report from Recurrent looked at over 30,000 EVs overall, and fewer than 4 percent had ever needed battery replacement, excluding major recalls of course. Recurrent used data from across several manufacturers and different model years, so it isn't exactly a Tesla-specific failure rate.

While Tesla keeps its pricing under wraps, Earthling Automotive's 2025 pricing breakdown paints a pretty clear picture of how much you'd pay for a new EV battery. Keeping taxes aside, as they vary from state to state, you could end up shelling out anywhere between $12,600 and $13,350 with installation to replace the battery pack on an older rear-wheel-drive version of the Model 3.

That number shoots up to $17,250 for the all-wheel-drive (AWD) Model 3, and if you own a 2016-to-2021 Model S or Model X, you could be parting with about $19,500 to $20,500. But remember, Earthling's installation charges aren't Tesla Service rates, so your final bill could look a lot different based on things like battery configurations, labor charges and other replacement parts.

In 2021, an invoice for a Model 3 battery replacement made the rounds online. The car had hit a large rock, so Tesla's warranty didn't cover the damage. The invoice listed a remanufactured battery at $13,500, and labor and add-ons brought the total to $16,550.67. If you'd rather not pay Tesla's prices, an independent EV specialist may be able to source a refurbished pack for cheap or repair specific faults, since an EV battery's life isn't always over once it's removed from your car. Still, your final bill depends on what's actually wrong with the battery, and it becomes a hard pill to swallow once it starts to match your aging Tesla's resale value.

Now, before you pull your hair out over signs that it's time to replace your EV battery, take your car in for a full diagnosis. Your best bet is getting Tesla to draw up an itemized bill, which will clearly show the battery cost (be it remanufactured or brand new) along with labor and other add-ons.

Before you pay that bill, though, check whether your warranty already covers it, since Tesla's battery and drive unit warranty stays with you for eight years or 100,000, 120,000 or 150,000 miles, whichever comes first. The mileage limit depends directly on your EV's model and configuration, and Tesla promises at least 70 percent battery capacity retention while the warranty lasts. If your Tesla falls below that threshold, you could get a free repair or even a total battery replacement. If you somehow manage to wreck your battery or need a replacement after all, the new battery comes with a four-year or 50,000-mile parts warranty. And if for some reason Tesla swapped your battery for free under the original coverage, don't expect a fresh eight-year warranty period.

Even with all the support, if you're nervous about the most expensive part of your EV, send another $2,000 Tesla's way for the Battery Extended Service Agreement. You can get this for eligible Model 3 and Model Y cars before the original battery warranty runs out, and depending on what qualifies as a battery failure, you're covered with just a $500 service deductible. Mind you, this won't include regular wear and tear that every EV battery goes through over time. For the extra $2,000, you can add up to 24 months or 30,000 miles of added coverage to your old and faithful EV.

#254. Russian ornithologist jailed over small donations to Navalny's foundation

Sofia Rosenfeld has devoted her life to studying Arctic birds. A Russian court sentenced her to 3.5 years in a penal colony over donations to Navalny's foundation. Friends and family are fighting for her release.

Boris Rosenfeld shows DW a photo of him with his daughter Sofia and can't hold back tears. "This was the last time we saw her. Then she left for Moscow, and this whole case began," he says.

Helives in Israel, while Sofia is in Russia. For more than a month now, she has been behind bars on charges of financing extremism. The case goes back to two donations totaling 2,000 rubles (about $30) to the late opposition politician Alexei Navalny'sAnti-Corruption Foundation (FBK), which the Russian authorities have since designated as extremist.

On October 7, a court in Moscow sentenced Rosenfeld to three and a half years in a penal colony.

Rosenfeld is a prominent ornithologist who has devoted her life to studying and protecting Arcticbirds. "Sofia was an avid young naturalist from childhood. She loved birds, horses and dogs," her father said as he leafed through a photo album.

Sofia was a teenager when the family moved to Israel but she returned to Russia a few years later and now holds both Russian and Israeli citizenship.

She studied biology at Moscow State University and developed a significant scientific career in Russia. Her colleague, Alexandra Panyutina, who now also lives in Israel, explained that Rosenfeld was devoted to her work from an early age.

"Birds and the Arctic are the defining passions of her life," she said.

Rosenfeld was among the first Russian researchers to develop a systematic approach to monitoring migratory bird populations. To support her research, she even developed a special aircraft.

"They could fly at almost the same speed as the birds and observe them from a low altitude," says Dmitry (name changed), a colleague of Rosenfeld's. "It quickly became clear that this was a unique method."

Rosenfeld is considered to be one of the leading figures in Russian ornithology. Her work has extended well beyond Russia and she has been deeply involved in international research projects. In the field of migratory bird conservation, cross-border cooperation is essential.

Helmut Kruckenberg, the head of the German Institute for Wetlands and Waterbird Research (IWWR), said Rosenfeld was highly respected within the international scientific community.

"She has done an enormous amount for nature conservation and for the protection of Siberian and Arctic species," he said. "What is happening to her is simply beyond comprehension for us."

In the summer of 2021, when Russian authorities designated Alexei Navalny's Anti-Corruption Foundation, also known as FBK, as an extremist organization, Rosenfeld was on a remote Arctic expedition without a phone or access to the internet. Therefore, she did not cancel her regular donations to the FBK immediately, doing so only after her return to the Russian capital Moscow.

Her friend Olga (name changed) described Sofia as a person of absolute honesty. According to her, Rosenfeld's donations to Navalny's foundation reflected a genuine desire to fight corruption. Through her work in Russia's regions, she had seen plenty of it firsthand.

"She was never involved in political activism. Her donations were solely intended to support anti-corruption work," said her father Boris Rosenfeld. "It's unthinkable".

For him and others close to her, the sentence came as a shock. Although prosecutors had requested a five-year prison term, friends and colleagues expected that she would receive a fine at most.

There were reasons for that expectation. According to calculations by independent media outlet Mediazona, about 85% of convictions in the 225 cases involving donations to Navalny's foundation have so far resulted in non-custodial sentences. Yet Rosenfeld got three and a half years in a penal colony.

Just a few months after Rosenfeld defended her doctoral dissertation in October 2025, her home was searched. She was also subject to travel restrictions. She continued to work but she had to cancel her annual summer expedition to the Arctic.

Even on the day of the sentencing, her conversations with  her colleagues focused largely on science:  "We discussed how the work could continue in Sofia's absence," Olga said. "But no one really believed she would end up in prison."

"The only thing we think about now is how to bring her here," Boris Rosenfeld says as he looks at the pictures from Sofia's last visit.

Friends and colleagues who spoke to DW say that his daughter never considered leaving Russia, even as the prospect of a prison sentence loomed. "Sofia would never have left. She simply can't imagine life without geese," says Dmitry.

Now, her family, friends and colleagues are campaigning to have her sentence overturned. More than 1,000 people have signed an appeal to Russia's Presidential Council for Human Rights.

Boris Rosenfeld is also hoping for support from Israel but so far Israeli consular officials have not been granted access to his daughter in detention.

The two continue to write to each other and he is trying to keep his spirits high: "She writes that she's trying to adjust to life in prison, and that it's hard," he says. "But she's a strong person."

This article was originally published in Russian.

#253. Tidal is banning AI-generated music entirely

The company expects to purge 29 million tracks.

Tidal will soon become the first streaming service to take a decisive stance against AI-generated music. On Tuesday, the company announced it would begin removing wholly genAI tracks from its catalog come December 9. According to platform lead Robert Anderson, Tidal's decision will result in the deletion of approximately 29 million tracks, and set the service on the path to reject 80,000 to 85,000 songs daily. "We believe this will resonate with both artists and listeners alike, as 96 percent of all AI-generated songs receive zero plays at all," Anderson wrote on X. "We are the first DSP to do so, and we encourage our peers to follow suit."

The move comes after Tidal announced earlier this year it would demonetize all fully AI-generated track, and label every such song as either AI-generated or AI-assisted. On Tuesday, however, Anderson said even that policy hasn't been enough to combat the deluge of AI tracks that has been flooding Tidal in recent months. Over the last 90 days, 43 percent of all tracks uploaded to the service were flagged as AI-generated, according to the company.

A few months ago, @Tidal tagged and demonetized all wholly AI-generated tracks to protect the authenticity of real artists. But that's enough, as 43% of tracks distributed to us in the last 90 days have been detected as AI-generated. Something more drastic needs to be done...

That Tidal should be the first streaming service to ban AI content is somewhat surprising. Block, the company that has owned Tidal since 2021, is led by AI enthusiast Jack Dorsey. At the start of the year, Block made headlines when it laid off 4,000 of its 10,000 employees, with Dorsey attributing the decision entirely to AI. "The core thesis is simple. Intelligence tools have changed what it means to build and run a company," he wrote at the time. "A significantly smaller team, using the tools we're building, can do more and do it better."

The only other streaming platform besides Tidal to outright ban music "generated wholly or in substantial part by AI" is Bandcamp. Spotify, for instance, has tried to dance around the issue; in October, the company said it would continue to remove "slop and spam" from people's recommendations, but it did this shortly after announcing it would also allow people to remix and cover songs using AI. Soundcloud got into bed with AI music creation companies Elevenlabs and Moises; its current policies try to balance the removal of spam with allowing AI tools to proliferate. Deezer added a toggle to hide (but not delete) AI-made music, while Apple Music merely labels songs made with AI.

This year, Black Friday falls on Nov. 27. While retailers often start featuring their best markdowns on Black Friday itself, there are plenty of early deals worth shopping in the lead-up. Most retailers' official sales do start well before the big day, so shopping strategically ahead of time can save you from missing out on a deal entirely (or dealing with the chaos the day after Thanksgiving).

Cyber Monday takes place on the Monday following Thanksgiving. This year, the shopping event takes place on Monday, Nov. 30. While Cyber Monday originally began as an online counterpart to in-person shopping on Black Friday, the two events have merged into an extended online shopping bonanza.

The mega-retailer just wrapped up its October Prime Day sale, and naturally, it's also getting in on the Black Friday action. For 2026, Amazon's official Black Friday sales kicked off on Nov. 19, which means deals are already live. Amazon has an incentive to spread out the shopping (to give its delivery drivers a break), so you no longer have to wait until Thanksgiving to save. Deals will continue to go live through Nov. 30

Amazon: Amazon recently announced that its Black Friday sale will begin on Nov. 19, with new deals dropping through Cyber Monday, on Nov. 30.

Best Buy: The big box store is hosting its Early Black Friday Deals + Doorbusters sale from Nov. 6 through Nov. 18, and the official Best Buy Black Friday sale kicks off on Nov. 19 and runs through Nov. 28. The Best Buy Cyber Monday Sale Event runs for 48 hours on Nov. 29 and Nov. 30.

Walmart: Walmart has three major sale events throughout November: the early Black Friday sale from Nov. 12 to Nov. 15, the Black Friday sale from Nov. 23 to Nov. 29 (with deals online only from Nov. 23 to Nov. 26), and the online-only Cyber Monday sale from Nov. 30 to Dec. 2.

Target: Target hasn't released its full Black Friday lineup yet, but we do know its first Early Black Friday sale kicks off Nov. 5 to Nov. 7. From Nov. 1 to Dec. 24, Target's Deal of the Day offer kicks off, featuring new deals every day. Every weekend after Nov. 7, the retailer will also drop new limited-time holiday offers.

#251. Porsche 718 Boxster prototype drive: This electric roadster is real

Technical details are still limited, but we already know it’s fun to drive.

It wasn’t until I was stuck in traffic on the way back from a run up and down some canyon roads that I realized just how low Porsche’s upcoming all-electric 718 Boxster truly is. I was idly looking around at the other cars, doing the math on the EV adoption rate in this small sample of Los Angeles gridlock (roughly 50 percent, impressively) when I noticed that I was eye-level with a Tesla Model Y door handle.

That’s not particularly low for a sports car, but it’s practically unheard of for an EV. Nearly all modern electric cars are built atop a skateboard-style battery pack, a stack of cells that elevates the seating position by a good 3 inches. In these SUV-heady days, that’s usually not a problem, possibly even an advantage. But, in a car like this, the closer you can get your keister to the road, the greater the sensation of speed.

So, for the company’s first all-electric sports car, the 718 Boxster that will be fully revealed next year, Porsche engineers put the battery pack behind the driver. That powers a single motor spinning the rear wheels and creates a driving experience that both honors the simple joy of motoring in a mid-engined Boxster while pushing the 718 to new heights of power and performance.

That EV battery layout, stacked behind the two-seat cabin rather than sandwiched below it, isn’t novel. It’s the same setup that Tesla used on the original Roadster back in 2008. Back then it was done for cost reasons as much as anything, enabling Tesla to repurpose a Lotus chassis meant to hold an internal combustion engine in the middle.

For Porsche’s new Boxster (and the Audi Concept C, which is built on the same platform), that pack enables the low seating position and also delivers a rearward weight bias (40:60 front/rear) that’s in keeping with the last-generation 718 Boxster, the internal combustion model killed by EU cybersecurity regulations last year.

Porsche isn’t saying how big the new roadster’s battery is in terms of charge capacity, only that its size was chosen to balance range and weight. We also don’t have an idea of rated range, charging speed, nor battery composition, but I can say the battery pack is based on an 800 V architecture like the electric Macan, so hopefully we can expect charging performance that at least matches that SUV’s 270 kW.

The new Boxster also shares a motor with the Macan. Porsche is not quoting any specs yet, but it puts out about 500 hp (370 kW) to the rear wheels on the Macan Turbo. You can place your bets on whether the Boxster application will result in more or less power. I would take the over, but regardless, it’s enough to sprint this electric roadster to 62 mph (100 km/h) in under 3.0 seconds, making it the quickest Boxster ever.

But it’s also the largest and heaviest. I was told the new Boxster’s curb weight will be somewhere in the ballpark of a current-generation 911, so in the region of 3,300 to 3,700 pounds (roughly 1,500 to 1,700 kg), meaning it has gained at least a few hundred pounds. That’s light for an EV but heavy for a roadster. Its wheelbase has grown accordingly.

You can absolutely feel that on the road. The 718 just doesn’t have the same buzzy eagerness as the latest 718 Boxster or Cayman. But that doesn’t mean it’s less fun to drive. In fact, I think most people would say it’s much more fun. Nearly doubling the old car’s base power output will do that.

This car, though, is about a lot more than acceleration. It still turns and handles incredibly well, borrowing much of its suspension, steering, and even chassis from the current-generation 911. Few would call a 911 a boring car, and the 718 is a step more aggressive even than that coupe.

That’s in part thanks to the response afforded by the electric powertrain, which isn’t saddled by the lazy throttle application caused by turbochargers and modern emission regulations. It’s sharper even than the latest 911 GTS, which required a trick electrically assisted turbocharger plus a battery and electric motor to bring the EV feel to a car driven by internal combustion.

To bring some of the charm of internal combustion to an EV, Porsche followed in the footsteps of the Hyundai Ioniq 5N by adding synthesized shifting and engine noises to the mix. Many cringe at the thought of an EV wailing unnecessarily, but having driven many battery-powered machines that make gas-powered noises, I can say with assurance that they always dial up the fun factor.

What they often lack is authenticity. Porsche sampled the sound of what its engineers determined was the sweetest-sounding 718: the 981-generation Boxster GTS. The new 718 Boxster replicates both that car’s 3.4 L flat-six and its seven-speed dual-clutch transmission, controlled by the paddles behind the steering wheel.

Enable the system, which Porsche calls E-Shift, then put the Boxster into launch control, and you’re in for a bit of a show: The car not only sounds like it’s bouncing off of a rev limiter, but the car itself actually shakes. It does this by pulsing the electric motor, vibrating in much the same way that the original Harley-Davidson Livewire did.

Lift off the brake and the Boxster blasts forward, again doing the sprint to 60 in less than 3 seconds. All the while, the pretend engine is screaming and running through its mock gears, either automatically or at your command with the paddles. In manual mode, the car will hit that artificial rev limiter and abruptly stop accelerating, so you’d better be quick to grab that next gear.

This whole system is there to add a greater sense of emotion to the car, but it does serve a practical purpose. Slinging the 718 around the tight, twisty circuit at the Los Angeles Porsche Experience Center, I was better able to judge my speed through corners by listening to the pretend engine that sounded all the world like it was spinning happily behind my head.

Don’t like it? Press the blue button on the steering wheel and it all goes away, but I have a feeling most people will want it on, at least when they’re driving for fun. They will certainly want it on when cruising into their local Cars & Coffee, since you can hear the sound outside the car as well as on the inside.

Cruising is better in the new 718 than the older model as well. Its adaptive suspension, dialed down to Normal mode, handles concrete separation joints on the highway and bumpy roads without issue.

And it offers something extremely rare on the EV scene: true drop-top motoring. The top folds itself down in somewhere around 10 seconds, tucking itself neatly on top of that battery pack. It also offers reasonable practicality, with a frunk in the nose plus a decently wide if shallow trunk out back. Both are roughly big enough to handle a carry-on suitcase or a couple of backpacks. That’s about it, though. There’s effectively no room behind the seats.

So, from a lifestyle perspective, it’s a bit more flexible and a bit more comfortable than the previous-generation Boxster, and from a power and aggression standpoint, it’s on another planet. Still, there’s no hiding that increase in weight and wheelbase. This truly feels like a cross-breed between a Boxster and a Carrera, which will disappoint some purists, but if you had to pick a pair of parents for a new model, you could do a lot worse than those two.

#250. HSBC's top execs face tense shareholders calling for a breakup

HSBC’s top brass defended their strategy Monday to frustrated shareholders in the lender’s largest market, as Europe’s biggest bank continued to face calls to be split up.

At an informal shareholder meeting in Hong Kong, Chairman Mark Tucker and CEO Noel Quinn took questions from investors on issues ranging from how the bank was approaching demands for an overhaul of its business to its purchase of Silicon Valley Bank’s UK arm.

In prepared remarks, Tucker and Quinn each reiterated the board’s recommendation that shareholders vote against a resolution on the docket for its annual general meeting in May that would force the bank to come up with a plan to spin off or reorganize its Asian business — the lender’s main source of profits.

HSBC's biggest shareholder reignites debate about breaking up the bank

Tucker said the board was unanimous in its opposition to the resolution, stating plainly: “It would not be in your interest to split the bank.”

He said the board had previously reviewed a range of options for restructuring the bank, and concluded that such alternatives would “materially destroy value for shareholders,” including dividends.

“Our strategy is working,” Tucker told the room of more than 1,000 shareholders. “Our current strategy is moving dividends up.”

HSBC has been facing calls to separate its Asian business from the rest of the bank over the past year.

Shareholders in Hong Kong — where HSBC is a mainstay of many retail investors’ portfolios — contend that the London-based lender’s performance has been dragged down by its businesses in other regions.

Quinn addressed those complaints head-on Monday, saying “our profits in Hong Kong and the UK are no longer being dragged down by underperformance elsewhere. The group is performing well as a whole.”

Pressed later by a shareholder on the issue, Quinn said a breakup of the bank would result in “significant revenue loss” because much of its business relied on cross-border transactions.

Investors have also been unhappy with HSBC scrapping its dividend in 2020, at the request of British regulators. They argue that if the lender cordoned off its activities in Asia, it would no longer have to expose Hong Kong shareholders to requests in other jurisdictions.

Christine Fong, a district council member in Hong Kong, said she represented about 500 small shareholders who had been affected by the dividend cancellation.

“Street hawkers, taxi drivers or teachers — they all relied on the dividend to pay for their regular expenses, like mortgage, insurance payments, school fees,” Fong told CNN.

“That’s why, three years ago, what HSBC did upset those small minority shareholders.”

Fong has now joined calls for shareholders to vote in favor of the proposal for the bank to spin off its Asian business, despite the lender bringing back its dividend in 2021, albeit at a lower level.

Ken Lui, an activist shareholder in Hong Kong who put the resolution together, doubled down on his call for support ahead of the meeting Monday.

The resolution will require 75% of votes to be passed in May, but “nothing is impossible,” he told reporters outside the meeting venue.

Lui, who said he personally held a stake worth 100 million Hong Kong dollars ($12.7 million), laid out plans for his team to focus on “targeted outreach to institutional shareholders to present our case and gain their support.”

His group will also canvass 18 districts of Hong Kong “to tell HSBC shareholders that they finally have a chance to speak for themselves and protect their rights through voting,” he added.

HSBC is also facing pressure from its largest shareholder.

Ping An (PNGAY), China’s biggest insurer, holds an 8% stake in HSBC and has backed calls for the bank to rethink its structure.

In a series of remarks made public by the Chinese firm last November, Huang Yong, chairman of Ping An’s asset management arm, said “we will support any initiatives including a spinoff that are conducive to improve HSBC’s performance and value.”

Since then, the insurance giant’s views haven’t changed, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The source told CNN that Ping An has been calling for HSBC to explore a reorganization, with an eye on boosting its valuation and simplifying its regulatory obligations around the globe.

The insurer has not recommended a specific path forward but will support any initiatives, including a spinoff of its Asian business, that could boost its stock performance or value, the person added. Ping An did not immediately respond to a request for comment on how it planned to vote at the upcoming general meeting.

HSBC’s leaders were also asked Monfday why the bank had scooped up the British unit of SVB following the stunning collapse of its parent in the United States. The purchase was made for £1 ($1.20) last month, just days after SVB had folded.

Critics have questioned HSBC’s ability to perform adequate due diligence on SVB UK’s customers because of how quickly the deal came together.

“Did HSBC look into the clients of SVB in detail? Say, the financial statement — whether they can pay back the loan?” said Fong.

HSBC buys SVB's UK business, ending 'nightmare' for British tech

Quinn and Tucker defended the acquisition, calling it a good business opportunity that allowed the bank to gain hundreds of innovative startups as customers. They pushed back on the notion that management hadn’t had time to carry out proper due diligence.

Tucker also weighed in on recent tumult in the banking industry, saying he did not expect an “immediate impact” on HSBC.

“After the collapse of a number of smaller regional banks and the takeover of Credit Suisse, the share prices of all banks have been suppressed,” he noted.

But he said he did not believe such developments represented “a systemic risk” to the sector. “I do expect a period of uncertainty” before nerves settle, he added.

#249. Germany's religious freedom report: Authoritarian regimes, holy wars, and spies abroad

Harassment, persecution, surveillance: Across much of the world, people of faith are facing growing pressure. A new German government report is unusually direct in criticizing China in particular.

The report spans more than 150 pages, but its conclusion can be summed up in a single sentence: "The global situation regarding freedom of religion and belief deteriorated during the reporting period," said Thomas Rachel, the German government's commissioner for freedom of religion and belief, and a member of parliament for the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU). Recently adopted by the Cabinet, the government's fourth report on the subject covers developments from 2023 to 2025.

The government has issued a dedicated report on freedom of religion and belief around the world. According to the report, this freedom is facing "increasing pressure" globally. The focus is not primarily on the suppression of religious institutions or structures, but on the situation of individuals who hold a religious belief, or none at all.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The importance of religious freedom is reflected in the way the government commissioner describes the issue: "Religion and faith are of great importance to four out of five people around the world and are central to their identity. People wake up with God and go to sleep with God. It is part of their everyday lives." Research by the Pew Research Center suggests that about 84% of the world's population identifies with a certain religion.

At a time when authoritarian regimes are gaining ground and expanding their surveillance capabilities, the report paints a bleak picture. The growing number of violent conflicts, the rise of authoritarian rule, and the spread of populism have led to "painful restrictions on freedom of religion and belief around the world."

The German government report does not attempt to provide a statistical tally of attacks or the number of people facing persecution. Instead, it examines 30 countries as case studies where, in the federal government's view, freedom of religion and belief is being restricted. These include about six countries each from Africa, Asia, and the Arab world. In Europe, the report focuses on Belarus, Russia, Ukraine, and Turkey, while in Latin America it highlights Mexico, Nicaragua, and Cuba. It also identifies shortcomings in five of the world's six most populous countries: China, India, Indonesia, Pakistan, and Nigeria.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Regarding India, the report refers to "Hindu nationalist efforts" that threaten the equal treatment of all officially recognized religions. It states that the generally peaceful coexistence of different faiths is "repeatedly overshadowed by tensions and, at times, violence." Both Muslim and Christian communities report growing intolerance and hate speech. According to the report, violent Hindu extremist groups have carried out a "large number of physical attacks" against Muslims, while the police and government authorities often respond inadequately.

In China, the German government identifies a "significant tightening of the legal framework of state control at the expense of freedom of religion and belief." According to the report, this particularly affects Uyghurs, Tibetans and churches that lack official state approval and are subject to harsh measures by the authorities. The law on the "Promotion of Ethnic Unity and Progress," which came into force on July 1, 2026, subordinates religion to "the formation of national identity" and patriotic education.

One of the countries where the situation has deteriorated most dramatically is Nicaragua, which has severely restricted freedom of religion and belief since 2018. The repression has primarily targeted the Catholic Church. According to the report, "intimidation, persecution, imprisonment, and expulsion" have forced around 130 priests and nuns to leave the country.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The reports reserves some of its sharpest criticism for Kirill, the patriarch of the Russian Orthodox Church. Under his leadership, the church has strongly supported Russia's war against Ukraine and portrayed it as a "holy war." According to the report, "weapons are blessed, Russian soldiers are absolved of their sins, and donations are collected for the war." It is perhaps the clearest example in the report of how religion can be used to justify oppression and violence.

The report explicitly addresses the threat posed by "transnational repression" (TNR), which it describes as a "growing global problem" that also affects Germany. The term refers to the persecution or intimidation of individuals by their country of origin beyond its own borders.

Ultimately, it argues, this amounts to a "continuation of domestic repression." Such "cross-border repression" has become considerably easier through the growing availability of digital means of repression, including smear campaigns on social media and spyware.

These forms of pressure range from physical attacks on individuals to digital assaults such as online intimidation and defamation. In some cases, repression is also carried out by threatening family members who remain in the country of origin. Russia and Iran, for example, are identified as the "main perpetrators of transnational repression" in Germany.

China is a particularly prominent example of religious and ideological tensions. Repression by Beijing in Germany primarily targets members of groups that the country's Communist Party classifies as "hostile to the system." These include Uyghurs, Tibetans, and members of the Falun Gong movement. According to the report, they are "also subject to surveillance and repressive measures in Germany," while relatives living in China are pressured.

Thomas Rachel hopes the newly published report will be "discussed in as many Bundestag committees as possible" and that members of parliament will "engage with the issue accordingly." Previous government reports on the subject have been debated in the Bundestag plenary at least once and, in some cases, twice.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The issue's place within the German government has also changed during the current legislative term. Commissioner Thomas Rachel is now based at the Foreign Ministry, while both of his predecessors since 2018 were attached to the Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development. Today, Rachel says, the importance of religion is being "taken into account" in German foreign policy. He also points to his involvement in the Foreign Ministry's diplomatic training programs.

In doing so, the government led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) reversed a structural decision made by the previous center-left coalition, which was led from 2021 to 2025 by Chancellor Olaf Scholz of the Social Democratic Party (SPD). The Scholz government had reduced the issue's prominence by assigning it to the "Religion and Foreign Policy" division. Religion and foreign policy have now regained a more prominent place within government.

One example is the current foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, who has already visited the Vatican more often than his two predecessors combined. In addition, alongside Rachel, the ministry has for some time maintained a dedicated unit headed by an ambassador that deals with, among other things, "fundamental issues relating to religion and foreign policy."

#247. Ways you can help your video doorbell stay charged in the winter

Winter can be tough on battery-powered video doorbells, but a few adjustments may help yours cope when temperatures drop.

While video doorbells aren't a necessity per se, it can be hard to imagine living without them once you own one. Knowing who's at the door saves you run-ins with unwanted salesmen. More seriously, they may help deter burglars — or help you catch an offender in the act if deterrence fails. Of course, your ability to capture that activity will depend in part on the distance at which your video doorbell stops detecting motion.

Another catch is that they're perpetually outdoors. That might not be such a big deal if you live somewhere warm like Miami or San Antonio. But in places with prolonged cold weather, battery life can suffer to the point that a video doorbell becomes more of a burden than an aid. It's inherent to the chemistry of lithium-ion technology, unfortunately.

The main way to alleviate this issue is by bringing your doorbell or its battery in from the cold. There may be other tactics you can employ, though, such as strategic positioning.

The critical point here is that an ideal charging range for lithium-ion batteries is between 50 and 86 degrees Fahrenheit (10 to 30 Celsius). When charging below the freezing point, there's a risk that metallic lithium will start plating onto electrodes, permanently reducing capacity. And even if the weather is slightly above freezing, charging will be less efficient than it could be. Cold-weather performance is one of the differences between sodium and lithium-ion batteries.

Before you charge a doorbell battery, make sure to let it warm up to room temperature first. This should not only preserve capacity but also help avoid cold-related charging delays. That's significant, considering that a Ring battery can take as long as 10 hours to top up. Let the battery charge fully before putting it back outside to maximize the time between recharges. If your doorbell has a removable battery, keeping a charged spare will minimize downtime. Some models in Ring's updated battery-powered doorbell lineup feature quick-release battery packs to make swaps easier.

Some doorbells don't offer removable batteries, however. One example is the battery-powered Google Nest Doorbell. In that case, you'll need to become familiar with removing your doorbell and bringing it indoors. Be sure to time this properly. Since a recharge might take several hours, it's probably wise to charge overnight unless you're worried about security and don't have any other cameras covering the front of your home.

In climates with borderline winters — that is, where the temperature only occasionally dips below freezing — you may be able to extend battery life by aiming or sheltering your doorbell in just the right way. If you can block the wind, for example, or maximize sunlight, your doorbell will naturally run warmer than it might otherwise.

A vital point here is that in extreme cold, it's possible for a doorbell to stop functioning for the duration. Anker, Ring, Google and others all agree on a minimum operating temperature of -4 degrees Fahrenheit (-20 Celsius). Between that and the freezing point, devices may still refuse to charge in order to prevent the plating we mentioned earlier.

Honestly, then, the best choice if you live in a frostbitten region may be to switch to a wired doorbell, as long as you can find one compatible with your home's design. While wired doorbells may still encounter problems around the -4 degrees Fahrenheit mark, they're otherwise immune to the cold, since they draw on the same electricity as the rest of your house.

#246. Unauthorized GTA 6 PC port shut down by Rockstar Games parent company

Don't try to port Grand Theft Auto VI to PC yourself — or you'll potentially find yourself in big legal trouble.

GTA 6 may finally be out on Xbox and PlayStation 5, but that doesn't help out the PC gaming faithful, who still have much longer to wait for their version of the game.

As a result, some impatient gamers have recently attempted to create PC ports of the game themselves. Notorious GTA 6 leaker, Cyberleek, also recently released an executable .exe file of the Xbox build of the game, which helped those efforts. Even without Cyberleek, these efforts were probably inevitable, as new AI tools have led to a surge in PS5 jailbreaks and unauthorized ports of classic video games.

However, Rockstar Games' parent company, Take-Two Interactive, clearly does not approve of these unofficial attempts to bring GTA 6 to PC ahead of schedule. On Monday, the company had the biggest GTA 6 PC port project, known as Leonida, taken down. So far, GTA 6 has generated billions of dollars, and the PC version could bring in billions more. And when it comes to protecting their IP, Take-Two and Rockstar aren't messing around.

GitHub, where the project was hosted, posted a Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) notice it received from Take-Two.

"We are the IP Enforcement Team for Take-Two Interactive Software, Inc., parent company of Rockstar Games," the notice reads. "We are writing to submit a takedown request regarding ItsNotRexed's GitHub repository and the 2900+ forks attached to it that infringes upon Take-Two's copyrighted works and facilitates copyright infringement of Rockstar Games title, Grand Theft Auto VI."

Take-Two explains how the project is based on the company's stolen IP, the Xbox version of GTA 6. "On November 20, 2026, stolen game files from an Xbox Series build of Grand Theft Auto VI were publicly distributed," the takedown notice reads. "The following day, this Leonida repository opened with the purpose of running the Xbox Series version of GTA VI on PC. Its README requires Xbox Series game files as input."

According to Take-Two, Leonida attempts to get around the IP issues by instructing project contributors to "bring your own files."

"This is intentionally misleading," Take-Two explains, pointing out that the files in question are the unauthorized GTA 6 files leaked by Cyberleek.

As our colleagues at PCMag point out, this is just one of many unauthorized projects attempting to bring GTA 6 to PC before the official version comes out. (Disclosure: Mashable and PCMag are both owned by the same parent company, Ziff Davis.) Other projects have reportedly managed to get the game's opening scene running on PC. Another has an extremely degraded version of the game running on Mac.

According to the Leonida project admin, Take-Two also successfully had the Discord server for the GTA 6 porting project taken down as well, so it does seem like the company is going to ramp up its takedowns of any attempted GTA 6 ports.

GTA 6 for PC has no official release date. However, GameBeat recently reported that the PC version may be released in early 2027, well before most gamers expected.

#245. Tidal announces ban on AI-generated music; 27 million tracks will be deleted

AI songs account for 6.3 percent of Tidal’s catalog, but it’s about to be zero.

Most streaming music providers have opted to label AI-generated content on their platforms, and until now, Tidal was one of them. However, the company is about to take a harder stance. Tidal announced that in the coming weeks, it will fully ban AI music because of the harm it does to human artists.

Tidal debuted its initial AI policy in July 2026, which included labeling and demonetizing all songs created entirely with AI. That wasn’t enough to stem the tide of AI slop, though. Over the past 90 days, Tidal reports that 43 percent of new uploads were completely AI-generated. On November 6, new uploads to Tidal hit a whopping 60 percent AI-generated.

As things stand, Tidal hosts 27 million tracks labeled as AI, all of which were obviously added in the past couple of years. That accounts for 6.3 percent of Tidal’s total catalog. On December 9, Tidal will delete all those songs. The streamer notes this will have essentially no negative impact, because 96 percent of AI-labeled tracks got zero plays in the past 90 days. Throughout its announcement, Tidal is careful to stipulate that it’s only talking about music that has been fully created by AI. Artists can still use AI tools as long as the final product contains human elements.

Credit: Tidal Credit: Tidal

Some people don’t particularly mind AI music, but the team at Tidal has come to believe the harm to artists is too great. AI models can pump out random noises faster than humans can create things of real value, which can mislead listeners and siphon royalty payments away from creators. There’s also an issue with AI uploaders who are actively attempting to steal royalty payments. Tidal says it has already removed about 66,000 tracks from its service for impersonating artists, which was against its AI policy even before this update.

As of December 9, individual uploaders and distributors will no longer be allowed to add AI music to Tidal. However, they could lie, couldn’t they?

Tidal hasn’t specified how it detects AI music, but it will probably rely on watermarking. Almost every AI song on Tidal (94 percent) comes from Suno, which added watermarking earlier this year. Tidal also cites Google Lyria as a source of AI tunes, which has SynthID labels embedded in the waveform. Deezer claimed it has a licensable AI music detector with a false-positive rate of less than 0.01 percent, but it’s unclear if Tidal is using that or something similar.

That will take care of most AI music, but this approach won’t detect everything. There are open models for music generation that you can run locally on a GPU, and some cloud-based providers aren’t bothering to watermark their outputs. Even if Tidal is using a separate detection system, new models may be able to evade it—it’s always going to be a cat-and-mouse game. This will be a problem with verifying provenance in all types of media in the future. For the time being, at least, Tidal’s policy should clear out most of the AI slop.

The people directing robots to make these songs will have plenty of other options after Tidal blocks AI. Spotify, YouTube Music, Deezer, and Apple Music all allow AI music on their platforms with labeling. Spotify has removed millions of AI tracks from its collection based on user feedback. Other streamers haven’t specified how much slop (if any) they’ve cleared out.

#244. China Renaissance suspends trading, delays results after founder's disappearance

China Renaissance, a top dealmaker in the country’s tech industry, said it would suspend trading of its shares and delay the release of its annual results because it still can’t get in touch with its founder.

Bao Fan, 52, started the boutique investment bank in 2005 and has been unreachable since the middle of February, according to the company. Shares in China Renaissance have plunged since Bao went missing, at one point dropping as much as 50%.

China Renaissance said in late February that it had learned Bao was “cooperating in an investigation” being carried out by certain authorities in the country. It gave no other details.

Chinese media have reported Bao might be assisting in an investigation related to a former executive at China Renaissance.

In a filing on Sunday, China Renaissance said auditors couldn’t complete their work or sign off on their report because of Bao’s absence. The board was also unable to give an estimate about when it would be able to approve its audited results for 2022 or dispatch its annual report by an April 30 deadline as required by Hong Kong’s listing rules.

Missing Chinese billionaire CEO assisting authorities in investigation, company says

Trading in the company’s shares was suspended from Monday as a result.

Bao is known as a veteran dealmaker who works closely with top technology companies in China. He helped broker the 2015 merger between two of the country’s leading food delivery services, Meituan and Dianping. Today, the combined company’s “super app” platform is ubiquitous in China.

His team has also invested in US-listed Chinese electric vehicle makers Nio (NIO) and Li Auto and helped Chinese internet giants Baidu (BIDU) and JD.com (JD) complete their secondary listings in Hong Kong.

Over the weekend, China’s top anti-graft watchdog launched an investigation into Liu Liange, former party secretary and chairman of Bank of China, according to a statement by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection and the State Supervision Commission. The bank is state-owned and one of the country’s four biggest lenders.

Liu is suspected of “serious violations of discipline and law,” the statement said. He is among the most senior financial executives targeted in a broader financial crackdown by President Xi Jinping.

In January, Wang Bin, former party chief and chairman of China Life Insurance, was charged by national-level prosecutors with taking bribes and hiding overseas savings.

#240. Taters and craters: Researchers say potatoes can grow in lunar soil

The goal of a self-sustaining lunar colony took a big step forward with the news that potatoes were successfully grown in simulated lunar soil.

The tubers were grown by Oregon State University researchers when they "amended" the simulated lunar dirt with organic material.

"We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter," Aymeric Goyer of Oregon State University’s Department of Botany and Plant Pathology said in a press release. "That's an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the Moon."

With its Artemis missions, NASA is barreling ahead with its plan for a sustained human presence on the Moon.

Earth's only satellite is covered by a layer of loose rock and dust called regolith, which contains heavy metals and very little organic matter. This makes self-sustaining farming on the Moon difficult. But adding organic matter, called vermicompost, to that lunar regolith can yield potatoes that are both edible and nutritious.

Organic matter can be produced by using earthworms to break down food scraps and plant waste. That vermicompost also helps bind the regolith's heavy metals together and makes the soil suitable for producing edible tubers.

Researchers tested five different regolith simulants to account for the Moon’s varied topsoil. The regolith containing 30 percent vermicompost yielded potatoes that matched those grown on Earth.

Studies are continuing on lunar potato production, with researchers looking at how 10 different varieties of potatoes grow in the moon’s soil.
