This year, why not get Dad a gift or two he won’t expect?

This year, why not get Dad a gift or two he won’t expect?

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Gone are the days when you could just buy your father a random tie or some leather-clad alcohol vessel or a shaving kit. Dads want — nay, deserve — something memorable. Luckily for you, it’s not that hard to find something special that he’ll approve of, and we’re here to guide you.

We’ve curated this year’s gift list with the modern father in mind, whether he’s a gamer, creator, chef, or simply a gadget lover. There’s a lot in here we think he’ll like, from noise-canceling headphones like the Sonos Ace Ultra and an autonomous drone to a brilliant QD-OLED monitor and a nifty light that’s perfect for illuminating his next campsite. Whatever your dad is into, we’ve got you covered.

Cleaning gadgets like Dyson’s PencilVac FluffyCones are never cheap, but they’re often worth the cost and a pleasure to use. The lightweight, broom-replacing stick vacuum doesn’t do carpets, but its rolling bars pack incredible cleaning power for touching up hard floors, including stairs.

Give the gift that fixes past home improvement transgressions. These handy Japanese-made pliers from Vampire Tools have one fundamental purpose — to remove stripped screws — and they’re damn good at it. The best part? Watching Dad’s face light up seconds before he sprints to the garage for them.

Who would have thought a simple hook could make roaming the city with a backpack so much more convenient? After testing Peak Design’s well-designed bags, we’re convinced the clever addition is a game-changer for anyone who doesn’t want to leave their bag on the filthy ground.

Give your father a little nostalgia and a lot of convenience in one package with this stylish USB-C dock and SSD combo gadget. The cassette-shaped Sharge Disk Pro 2 works as a hub with support for HDMI at 4K, SD and microSD card slots, USB-A and USB-C ports, along with up to 8TB of storage stored within.

It’s time to help Dad ditch his collection of plastic reusable cups, which have clearly seen better days. NotNeutral’s hand-pressed, timeless tumbler offers ’70s vibes with a modern twist, making it the perfect vessel for whatever Dad twists into his favorite drink.

For those who love travel but hate the constraints of a hotel TV, Belkin’s ConnectAir is a slick solution. Plug the transmitter into any device with a USB-C video-out port and the receiver into the TV’s HDMI port, and voilà, you’re easily (and wirelessly) connected.

Have you broken something fragile that seems impossible to mend? Maybe all you need is a Kintsugi Repair Kit, which provides the Japanese method and a special lacquer to repair and restore broken ceramics to good health. The resulting golden scar is merely to remind us that rebuilding is possible.

Werewolf’s affordable dongle kit provides an almost magical way to power nearly any DC device from a USB-C charger or portable battery. Program it from a mobile app, connect it to your old gear, and everything from a PC monitor to an original Game Boy can accept USB-C charging.

If your father already owns an Apple Watch, the Nomad Stratos is a foolproof upgrade idea. The refined watch band features titanium links with a rubbery interior for durable comfort, and it comes in an array of subtle color options that make it as suitable for the office as it is for the slopes.

If you’re after a cheap, useful stocking stuffer, Trond’s reliable three-prong extension cord is a practical pick that’s available in leftward or rightward configurations to fit nearly any outlet. Dad will probably say, “Oh, I’ve always wanted one of these,” and this time he’ll mean it.

The CS-Pro will make your dad feel like a private eye in the early ’80s. The retro-inspired digital camera serves up 16-megapixel stills and offers four filters accessible from its tactile dial, plus USB-C charging, a high-quality Xenon flash, and a 4GB SD card for plenty of vintage photo fun.

Antigravity’s A1 is the ultimate gadget for the dad who dreams of owning the sky. The compact drone comes with specialized goggles that will make him feel like he’s in the cockpit, and it records always-on, 360-degree 8K video. It’s an exhilarating flight experience and an excellent creator’s tool in one slick package.

Sonos raised its headphones game on all fronts with the Ace Ultra, which deliver better noise canceling, improved sound, and the feature we’ve all been waiting for: Wi-Fi support. With the ability to bounce audio across your Sonos ecosystem, including from a TV via newer Sonos soundbars, Dad’s sonic sanctuary is finally complete.

WiiM’s first soundbar builds on its seamless Sonos-esque connectivity with a sleek design, detailed sound, and up-firing speakers for Dolby Atmos spatial audio. It also pairs with other speakers for surround sound through a no-fuss setup process, including ones you already own that are linked to one of WiiM’s amplifiers.

Your dad needs an awesome monitor, but there are 10 billion options. Alienware’s 34-inch Penta Tandem QD-OLED delivers top-end picture quality, with vibrant colors and perfect blacks, plus a swift 280Hz refresh rate. Best of all, it’s not nearly as expensive as you might think.

If your dad is still reading books on his phone (or aging e-reader), it’s time for an upgrade. The latest in Amazon’s series of waterproof, auto-dimming e-readers loads books faster than the prior model and offers a slick aluminum upgrade. No matter which you choose, it’s a better way to bring the library along.

Oura didn’t reinvent the wheel with the Ring 5, but it did reshape it into a slimmer, thinner, more wearable design that could make all the difference. Inside are the same extensive health and fitness tracking features for charting everything from sleep to heart health, backed by long battery life.

Smart TVs are often pretty dumb. If your dad is always complaining about his TV, or if you want to get ahead of it, grab the latest Apple TV 4K. Although it’s not cheap, it stands out with built-in mics for Siri AI, lots of power, HomePod surround sound support, and a simple, ad-free interface.

The Switch 2 leverages the same ideas as its predecessor, only with a larger, 7.9-inch display, a faster chip, and a bevy of new social features. However, its most important trait is that it’s the newest Nintendo console, which means access to a host of weird, beautiful, family-friendly games that only Nintendo could dream up, now on a better screen.

BougeRV’s fancy, compact lamp will spark joy for the glamper in your life, as well as everyone else. Its powerful, foldable spread of LEDs provides a blast of light anywhere plug-ins can’t reach, from the beach to the shed where that scary spider holds court, with up to 60 hours of light on low power.

The Rival Pro offers plenty of thoughtful extras, including swappable batteries and an ultra-wideband base station for a seamless, low-latency connection. The gaming mouse’s lightweight design and 8,000Hz polling rate also deliver both accurate and ergonomic performance for up to 16 hours per charge.

For the manga or live-action Netflix show lover on your list, this fashionable Pirates jersey, inspired by Monkey D. Luffy from the seminal pirate adventure series One Piece, will be as surprising as it is delightful.

Zero Company, a strategy game set in the twilight of the Clone Wars, is a fun way to get lost in the Star Wars universe. The single-player, turn-based title lets players command a diverse team of characters across a gorgeous expanse of worlds, offering hours of solitary entertainment.

We fell for Apple’s handy iPhone strap due to its effortless accessibility and comfy design, which uses flexible magnets to keep excess segments in check. From biking to hiking to concerts, it’s a great way to sling your iPhone 18 Pro, assuming you have a compatible phone case.

The new Fitbit Air provides the same great fitness tracking we’ve come to expect in a comfortable design that virtually disappears on your wrist. Google’s AI Coach can be overly assertive, but the tracker’s great battery life and metrics for everything from sleep to blood oxygen make it an excellent gift for anyone who needs a healthy hand.

Most of us have thousands of photos in the cloud, but if a photo never makes it into the real world, did it really happen? Existentialism aside, the Cricut StickerPix offers a new way to play with photos, providing you with everything you need to turn any picture into a pro-quality print or sticker.

This battery-powered fan is a big upgrade over your average plug-in job. As a 3D circulator, it can tilt to push air in all directions. It can be controlled from an app and even detaches from its stand to sit on a desk or tabletop. Quiet, powerful, and versatile, it’s equipped for nearly any adventure on or off the grid.

If your favorite cinephile is looking to get off the streaming carousel, the Kaleidescape Strato E is the key. The premium player lets library builders locally store and play their favorite films and TV shows in lossless 4K resolution with Dolby Atmos for sterling entertainment that’s all theirs.

Once The Great British Baking Show becomes an obsession, only a serious stand mixer will do for replicating recipes at home. This mixer’s timeless design adds new features in what KitchenAid calls its biggest upgrade since 1955, with a new half-speed setting and a control lever that lets you set speeds between its standard settings.

The Pocket Scion is unlike any musical instrument you’ve witnessed before, one that uses the “biofeedback” from plants to trigger built-in synths. The device offers MIDI-out to send digital signals to outboard synths, and it includes an app for both macOS and Windows, finally giving you a way to make your favorite fern a rockstar.

When it comes to jotting down notes, there’s nothing like a pen and paper. At least, that’s what we thought before we tried the Remarkable Paper Pure. Offering a strikingly realistic writing experience that saves everything in the digital realm, this tablet is a brilliant way to bridge the gap and save paper.

Electronics are becoming more sustainable, and Fairphone is leading the way. The Fairphone 6 Plus may seem like a regular Android phone on paper, but the ability to repair and replace its internals, from the screen to the battery, makes it anything but average.

#161. Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'

Funding from wealthy countries to help deal with the impacts of climate change hasn't materialized, says Uganda's environment minister. The East African country is hoping oil and carbon credits will help boost finances.

Ugandan Environment Minister Beatrice Atim Anywar has come to the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, seeking to secure more funding for her country as it grapples with climate change.

"This is a thing we are living with," she told DW on the sidelines of the COP31 summit, where she's leading the Ugandan delegation. "People are displaced, people are dying of harm, hunger. It has implications on food security and livelihoods."

In recent years, the East African nation has been hit by a series of climate-related disasters, from deadly landslides and floods washing away villages, to droughts damaging harvests and hydroelectricity production.

"When we come to COP and we talk of what the reality is on the ground, we Ugandans have suffered it," Anywar said, referring to the effects of climate change.

"It has an implication for the health of our people, on national budgets," she added.

Climate financing for developing countries to deal with the impacts of a warming planet has become a major sticking point at this year's climate talks. The gathering of some 200 states is seeking to close gaps on how to scale up financing from developed states and whether support should be provided through grants or loans.

Africa contributes less than 4% of the global greenhouse emissions that drive rising temperatures globally, but the continent is among the most vulnerable to climate impacts.

As it deals with the effects of climate change, including extreme weather, Uganda is also rapidly expanding investment in electricity production from renewables such as hydropower and solar.

In the country of some 53 million people, more than 90% of Ugandan households still rely on wood and charcoal as the most affordable fuel for things like cooking. Biomass accounts for 90% of the country's final energy consumption.

While using wood and charcoal leads to deforestation, Ugandans have little choice. Only around 2% of the country's energy comes from electricity — which is largely derived from hydropower — and less than half of the population has access to electricity.

"Now we are deliberately going into scaling up the production of electricity — hydropower electricity — and making it cheaper for cooking," Anywar said. "We have other alternative energy sources... to mitigate this charcoal use. But the use needs to be phased out in a systematic manner by giving them alternatives."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

At the same time, the country is seeking to boost economic development by becoming an oil producer. Due to open in 2027, a controversial 1,443-kilometer (897-mile) pipeline is nearly complete. It connects two oil sites in eastern Uganda with a port on the Tanzanian coast.

Environmentalists have criticized the East African Crude Oil Pipeline project, which can transport up to 246,000 barrels per day. Environmentalists say it runs counter to the goal of limiting global temperature rise and could damage fragile ecosystems.

The Climate Accountability Institute said it would release 379 million tons of climate-heating pollution over its 20-year lifetime.

Oil wells for the project, operated by French energy giant TotalEnergies, are also located in Uganda's largest and oldest national park, Murchison Falls.

"That has been also a sticky issue. And actually, that is one of the challenges we are facing at COPs," Anywar said. She stressed that measures have been taken to limit emissions, and that the project was progressing in a "very deliberate way."

The minister also urged developed countries to cut less wealthy nations some slack for using the resources they have to drive much-needed development, saying oil revenues could help fund the transition to cleaner energy.

"You cannot tell us to cut off the umbilical cord that feeds us, as much as it has to be cut off," Anywar said, criticizing the lack of financing from developed countries to deal with climate change. "We are here begging for funds that are not forthcoming."

Anywar added that developing countries "need a just transition," referring to an equitable shift away from fossil fuels that focuses on protecting workers and communities.

Another way Uganda is looking to finance climate change adaptation is through carbon credits, Anywar said, describing them as a potential "breakthrough."

Carbon credits are tradeable permits representing one ton of carbon dioxide that has been reduced or removed from the atmosphere through initiatives such as forest protection, renewable energy projects or tree planting schemes. Companies or governments can buy them to offset emissions they have not cut themselves.

"Our country is rich with biodiversity. And that is what we are looking forward to — attracting investors into our natural setup so that we earn some finances," Anywar said.

Carbon credits have been promoted as an important source of income for developing countries. But they have also faced criticism, for a lack of transparency and allowing polluting activities to continue.

"We need to have a bankable approach to all interventions. Otherwise… it's not going to work for us," Anywar said, adding that her country also wants to attract investment and build partnerships in smart agriculture and the energy transition.

"If we rely on begging for funds which are not forthcoming, we shall go back empty handed."

#160. Threads comes to iPad and takes a page from X’s playbook with cashtags

It may have taken 15 years for Instagram to launch on the iPad, but Instagram’s other app, Threads, has taken a slightly faster path to the Apple tablet. In an overnight update, the company rolled out a big-screen version of the X competitor. It’s also added another new feature, borrowed from X: the stock-tracking feature known as cashtags.

While the iPad version of the app works well in portrait orientation, some users are disappointed to find that the landscape layout doesn’t work as they’d expect. Instead of offering a multi-column interface as on Threads’ web app, the iPad app focuses on the user’s main feed in a single-column layout. There are also options to swipe right and left from the main screen to access the search screen and the feeds menu, respectively.

The iPad app isn’t the company’s only update in the latest release. According to a post from Threads engineer Guy Dickinson, Threads will now support cashtags — a feature popularized by Twitter years ago for tracking live stock information. These specialized tags start with the dollar sign (“$”) followed by a ticker symbol. When you click on a cashtag, you can follow the discussions around the stock.

In addition, Threads is adding live stock quotes, charts, and other context at the top of each cashtag’s page. As you search for a particular cashtag, the autocomplete search results will display the stock’s current price and the percentage it’s up or down. Dickinson says the feature will currently support NYSE and Nasdaq stocks, ETFs, and crypto. Cashtags will be supported on the web, iOS, and Android. However, they’re just now rolling out, so you may not immediately see them.

The update points to Threads’ broader ambition to compete with X, not only as a destination for discussions about various topics, but also as a place where people can track real-time news and information. Cashtags in particular could attract traders and investors to Threads who typically rely on X.

Despite facing stiff competition from X, Meta announced earlier this year that Threads topped 500 million monthly users, and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg says the company believes the app is on track to reach a billion users over time.

The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) disclosed on Tuesday that it’s investigating a “cybersecurity incident.” The bureau, which is part of the Treasury Department, said it’s looking into an “incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems.” It hasn’t offered any information about the full scope or source of the breach, but FinCEN has taken some systems offline as a precaution.

The news comes hours after The New York Times reported that the Central Intelligence Agency and Office of the Director of National Security discovered a breach of an open source intelligence system, exposing unclassified information. The Department of Defense, whose National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency was also reportedly impacted by the breach, declined to comment. The CIA and ODNI did not immediately respond to requests for comment. It’s unclear if the FinCEN breach is related. Americans have been on high alert about security incidents after a series of seemingly unrelated outages earlier this month.

Americans have been on high alert about security incidents

FinCEN’s role is to protect the financial system from illegal activity, including by combatting money laundering and terrorism financing. The bureau maintains financial transaction data and distributes it for law enforcement purposes. FinCEN also houses reports of suspicious activity that financial institutions file as part of the Bank Secrecy Act.

FinCEN says in its alert that banks can still file reports about suspicious activity online, but some services may not be immediately available. Filers that need to expedite their reports in the meantime can still call the Financial Institutions Hotline, which it says was not impacted by the disruption.

#158. The $500 billion beauty industry's 'green' ambitions are a patchwork at best. And they're falling short

The escalating climate crisis is shifting many people’s purchasing patterns and this extends to the $500 billion dollar global beauty industry which is grappling with a range of sustainability challenges across product manufacturing, packaging and disposal.

'Delay means death': We're running out of ways to adapt to the climate crisis, new report shows. Here are the key takeaways

Strategy and consulting firm Simon Kucher’s Global Sustainability Study 2021 found 60% of consumers around the world rated sustainability as an important purchase criterion, and 35% were willing to pay more for sustainable products or services.

This shift in consumer preferences has propelled many beauty brands to set environmental goals: to move away from single-use and virgin plastics, provide recyclable, reusable and refillable packaging and offer more transparency around products’ ingredients so customers can ascertain how “green” their purchase is.

However, consumers still struggle to understand the sustainability credentials of many products, according to the British Beauty Council. This is because the industry’s clean-up efforts have been inconsistent, and fall short of making a recognizable impact in the absence of collective goal-setting, global strategy and standardized regulations.

There is no international standard for the beauty industry on how much product ingredient information to share with customers — or how to do so. Brands can set their own rules and goals, giving rise to confusion and “greenwashing,” where sustainability claims are often touted but not substantiated.

Companies often use marketing language like “clean beauty” to make it seem like their products are natural, for example, when they may not actually be organic, sustainable or ethically made.

After rebranding in the West, many beauty companies are still offering to 'whiten' skin elsewhere

“The term ‘clean beauty’ has become quite dangerous. It’s used to sell more products,” according to British Beauty Council CEO Millie Kendall, who added that such buzzwords are losing traction in the UK as British customers wise up to their shortcomings. “Customers need better marketing information and certification information.”

In a 2021 report calling on the industry to have “the courage to change” their business practices, the British Beauty Council wrote that, all too often, even natural ingredients involved in manufacturing products give way to “over-consumption, non-regenerative farming practices, pollution, waste and neglect.”

“The only way out of this is transparency,” Kendall told CNN.

Jen Lee, chief impact officer at US-based brand Beautycounter, said she continues to see confusion over ingredients among consumers. (In 2013, the company launched and published “The Never List,” which currently cites more than 2,800 chemicals — including heavy metals, parabens and formaldehyde — it claims to never use in its products.)

“Natural vs. synthetic ingredients has been a conversation. People think natural is safer, but it’s not always the case,” Lee explained. “Natural ingredients formulated in the industry can have toxic load. Heavy metals can occur in natural components of the earth.”

Mother loses peripheral vision from apparent exposure to mercury in beauty creams. Toxic levels in her home put family at risk, say experts

“We used to be more natural and organic,” added Sasha Plavsic, founder of makeup brand ILIA Beauty. “What was challenging is (that) raw materials were difficult to source or would come in inconsistently or products wouldn’t perform.”

Most makeup is created and molded at high temperatures, Plavsic explained. Purely organic materials often fall apart in this heat, leading to inconsistent results and subpar product performance. “Not every synthetic is bad,” Plavsic said. “Sometimes, it helps create the best in class formula.”

The industry’s plastic packaging is a particular sustainability challenge — 95% is thrown away and the vast majority is not recycled, according to the British Beauty Council.

The cosmetics business is the fourth biggest plastic packaging user globally — after food and beverage, industrial packaging and pharmaceuticals — and plastic is about 67% of the industry’s packaging volume, according to Vantage Market Research. Beauty giant L’Oreal used 144,430 metric tons of plastic in its packaging material in 2021, for example, according to the Ellen Macarthur Foundation (EMF). Estee Lauder Companies reported its brands produced 71,600 metric tons of plastic in product packaging that same year.

And only 9% of the global plastic waste is recycled, according to a report from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. The United States only recycles 4% of its plastic waste.

Single-use plastic is wreaking havoc on the planet. Here's what you can do to minimize your impact

Many brands are trying to phase out harmful plastics from their operations and adopt post-consumer recycled (PCR) plastic. (L’Oreal has set a target of 50% PCR plastic usage by 2025, while Estee Lauder is targeting 25% “or more” PCR plastic — but both are far from achieving their targets.)

“Between 60-70 major global brands have made unprecedented progress” in PCR plastic usage across industries, EMF’s Plastic Initiative Lead Sander DeFruyt told CNN. But DeFruyt stressed that PCR plastic must be adopted in conjunction with brands removing single and virgin plastics from their usage cycles to truly make a difference.

However, PCR plastic is not easy to find — low recycling rates around the world mean there is limited supply. Meanwhile, demand for it is growing demand across industries, DeFruyt said. This competition hikes up its price, which is already higher than virgin plastic.

Hair care brand FEKKAI claims that it used up to 95% PCR content in its packaging, but pricing and supply issues posed a challenge, forcing it to currently aim for containers and packaging that feature at least 50% PCR in its packaging.

“PCR plastic is more expensive than stock plastic. The cost is hard and then sourcing it is too,” founder Frédéric Fekkai told CNN. “PCR is close to our heart, but there is a massive demand, so finding recycled plastic is difficult.”

Beauty retailers plays a pivotal — and under-utilized — role, with control over stocking decisions and supply chains. But many vary when it comes to the standards they set for brands they sell.

“Smaller businesses do more, full stop,” said Jessi Baker, founder of the technology platform Provenance, which helps brands display their sustainability credentials for customers. “They move more nimbly. Some of them are born-good brands — climate friendliness was part of their setup. They don’t need to restructure their entire supply chain. Their culture already has it compared to the larger brands who need to work hard to change.”

A history of beauty trends -- and the standards that shaped them

Sephora launched its “Clean + Planet Positive” initiative in 2021, which labeled products that met its set criteria. (This is separate from the French retailer’s “Clean at Sephora” program, which is currently facing a consumer lawsuit alleging it carries a significant percentage of products understood by customers to be harmful.) Target launched a similar program in 2022, featuring a “Target Zero” icon for both online and in-store offerings that either have reusable, recyclable, compostable or reduced plastic packaging, or feature waterless or concentrated products.

Still, many steps taken by brands and retailers do not even begin to touch on the waste and pollution generated throughout supply chains, manufacturing and shipping, all huge problems for the industry to grapple with.

The gaps in standardization in the beauty ecosystem can, to some extent, be filled by certifications such as the US-born B Corporation, or B Corp. This accreditation, one of the most well-known in the beauty space, is issued by the non-profit B Lab, which scores a company on a variety of criteria around ethics and sustainability. However beneficial it may be among eco-conscious consumers, though, it is currently completely voluntary for brands to apply for.

Governments and multinationals enforcing regulations and setting a base line for brands to operate from when making sustainability claims would go a long way to making change, many experts and business leaders believe.

Susanne Kaufmann, founder of her namesake beauty brand, says her efforts in Austria would reap better results if more countries around the world had stricter, more uniform garbage disposal laws.

A trash heap 62 meters high shows the scale of India's climate challenge

“I package our product in a recyclable material,” Kaufmann said. (Her products’ packaging, which is refillable and reusable, is made from 75% recycled plastic — and is 100% recyclable.) If I send this to the US, the garbage is not separated… and it’s not recyclable,” she explained, referring to inconsistencies in recycling laws across the United States.

And when it comes to ingredients, the European Chemicals Agency lists 2,495 substances banned from use in cosmetic products marketed for sale or use in the bloc. But the US Food and Drug administration only lists 11, making it more challenging for American consumers to find safer, greener options. The Environmental Working Group, a non-profit watchdog, studied lab tests of 51 sunscreen products in 2021 and found that only 35% of products met the EU standard, compared with 94% that passed the US standard.

However, while government can set minimum requirements, Mia Davis, vice president of sustainability and impact at beauty retailer Credo Beauty, says the needle will move in the private sector.

Sustainable ships: The world's most eco-conscious cruises

“Regulation can raise the floor a bit. A person who doesn’t know about any (sustainability issues) should still be able to walk into a bodega and get clean products… But that’s never going to be what the market can do,” she said. “Market leadership is key.”

In the absence of bold regulations or global standards on sustainability practices, this “leadership” — undertaken both by brands and customers in the beauty marketplace — is likely to be the most immediately impactful vector for addressing the industry’s climate shortcomings. It will take continued collective advocacy and initiative to see meaningful climate-conscious change.

#156. UK warns AI-driven cyberattacks are exposing years of weak security

The U.K. government’s cybersecurity unit says it has seen a “marked rise” in AI-driven cyberattacks in recent months, as hackers increasingly rely on autonomous hacking tools to identify and exploit simple weaknesses to break into systems and networks.

The U.K. National Cybersecurity Center (NCSC) said it has seen several cyber incidents since September involving autonomous hacking tools, such as penetration testing tools used by defenders to stress-test their cybersecurity defenses. These incidents have caused intrusions at organizations and resulted in downtime, the unit said in a blog post.

The NCSC says that while none of the vulnerabilities being exploited are new, the speed at which these AI tools are able to carry out simple hacks has changed.

The rise in AI-related cyberattacks coincides with the broader release earlier this year of open source autonomous penetration testing tools like Artex and Cairn, among others, which anyone can download and use at no cost. The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation recently warned that malicious hackers are using AI penetration testing tools to carry out cyberattacks at unprecedented speeds.

While cyberattacks and intrusions are on the rise, the message from London is that many of these attacks are preventable with basic cybersecurity defenses and best practices.

“Notably, the issues being exploited currently are not novel memory corruption vulnerabilities (or even known but unpatched vulnerabilities), but unmitigated weaknesses that are often the result of years of technical debt that organisations have accumulated,” the NCSC wrote.

The unit said that agentic hacking tools often look for exposed or internet-facing systems, then quickly run through lists of weak or easy-to-guess passwords or abuse API endpoints often used by developers to access data.

The NCSC said that AI “does not make established cyber security controls obsolete,” but rather that “building strong foundations has never mattered more.”

The unit added that AI has made it easier to find vulnerabilities and faster to exploit them, warning that weaknesses that have gone unnoticed for years can now be found in minutes.

#155. North Macedonia remains stalled on its EU path after 21 years as a candidate

EU enlargement has regained momentum, with Montenegro and Albania moving closer to membership. But North Macedonia, a candidate since 2005, remains stalled by a politically difficult dispute involving Bulgaria.

The European Union's enlargement drive has regained momentum: Montenegro could become the bloc's 28th member in 2028, while Albania is rapidly advancing through accession talks and could complete accession negotiations by the end of 2027 if it maintains its current pace of reforms.

But North Macedonia, an EU candidate since 2005, remains stalled on the road to accession.

That contrast will be particularly evident at Wednesday's EU-Western Balkans summit in Brussels.

"The Western Balkans' future is in the European Union. Their accession is our priority, our shared ambition and a crucial geopolitical investment in these turbulent times," European Council President Antonio Costa said ahead of the meeting.

North Macedonia formally opened accession talks with the EU in July 2022 but has yet to open the first of the EU's six negotiating clusters, the groups of policy areas through which candidates align their laws and institutions with EU standards.

But the lack of movement does not mean the country is unprepared for membership.

EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said in November that North Macedonia was "among the countries with the highest level of preparedness" in aligning with EU law and had recently accelerated reforms under the EU Growth Plan.

However, she added, "the handbrake on its accession negotiations is still on."

Kos said that to release this handbrake and open the first cluster, North Macedonia must adopt the constitutional amendment agreed with the EU in 2022.

For years, a dispute with Greece over the country's name blocked North Macedonia's progress along the EU accession path.

Although the 2018 Prespa Agreement resolved the dispute, and the country changed its constitutional name, clearing the way for NATO membership, a breakthrough on EU accession did not follow.

Bulgaria later blocked the process amid disputes over history, language and identity. A compromise brokered during the French EU presidency in 2022 lifted the veto but made further progress conditional on North Macedonia amending its constitution to explicitly include Bulgarians among the country's recognized communities.

The amendment requires a two-thirds majority in parliament, which has so far proved unattainable.

From the EU's perspective, this is no longer a Bulgarian veto, but a condition North Macedonia accepted as part of its negotiating framework.

"It [North Macedonia] is not blocked by a member state. It is blocked because it doesn't want to date to do what it knows needs to be done," Gert Jan Koopman, the European Commission's director-general for Neighbourhood and Enlargement Negotiations, recently told an Atlantic Council podcast.

North Macedonia's government sees the problem differently.

EU membership remains its declared strategic goal, but Skopje wants guarantees that amending its constitution will not simply pave the way for further demands from Sofia.

Those concerns are rooted partly in long-running disputes over identity and history: Bulgarian governments have challenged North Macedonia's interpretation of a centuries-old distinct Macedonian identity, while some Bulgarian politicians have gone further, describing Macedonian as a regional variant of Bulgarian, and Macedonians and Bulgarians as one people.

President Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova says North Macedonia is ready for talks with Bulgaria and the EU but wants certainty that one constitutional change will not simply be followed by demands for another.

"We only want certainty. We only want this not to be yet another amendment for the sake of an amendment, followed by another one," she said.

After more than two decades of waiting, the deadlock has also become a domestic political problem in North Macedonia.

A nationally representative survey by the Institute for Democracy "Societas Civilis" illustrates the contradiction: 71% of respondents support EU membership, but only 24% back the constitutional amendments needed to advance the process. Among ethnic Macedonians, support for the amendments falls to just 11%.

Skopje-based political analyst Petar Arsovski describes the public mood as "passive-aggressive:" Strong support for joining the EU coexists with weak support for making the concession currently required to move forward.

That, he says, helps preserve the status quo.

The dispute is now deeply embedded in domestic politics in both North Macedonia and Bulgaria, where retreat from established positions could easily be portrayed as a national defeat.

The political cost is particularly high in Skopje, where the current government came to power in part on a platform of opposition to constitutional changes under the existing conditions.

For North Macedonia's government, accepting the amendments without further guarantees carries considerable domestic political risks.

The EU, meanwhile, is not offering to reopen the negotiating framework.

The uncertainty is compounded by debate over how future EU enlargement should work. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron have proposed allowing candidates to gradually gain some benefits of membership before formally joining, while stressing that full membership remains the ultimate goal.

According to Arsovski, uncertainty over the future course of enlargement gives ammunition to Eurosceptic narratives and reduces the political incentive for a difficult compromise.

"If these overall conditions remain unchanged, the most likely scenario is that EU summits come and go, while political actors remain dug in, with no real convergence of positions and no genuine commitment to a substantive compromise," Arsovski told DW.

#154. Hundreds of millions at risk from Chinese shopping app malware

It is one of China’s most popular shopping apps, selling clothing, groceries and just about everything else under the sun to more than 750 million users a month.

But according to cybersecurity researchers, it can also bypass users’ cell phone security to monitor activities on other apps, check notifications, read private messages and change settings.

And once installed, it’s tough to remove.

In a detailed investigation, CNN spoke to half a dozen cybersecurity teams from Asia, Europe and the United States — as well as multiple former and current Pinduoduo employees — after receiving a tipoff.

Multiple experts identified the presence of malware on the Pinduoduo app that exploited vulnerabilities in Android operating systems. Company insiders said the exploits were utilized to spy on users and competitors, allegedly to boost sales.

“We haven’t seen a mainstream app like this trying to escalate their privileges to gain access to things that they’re not supposed to gain access to,” said Mikko Hyppönen, chief research officer at WithSecure, a Finnish cybersecurity firm.

“This is highly unusual, and it is pretty damning for Pinduoduo.”

This is highly unusual, and it is pretty damning for Pinduoduo.

Malware, short for malicious software, refers to any software developed to steal data or interfere with computer systems and mobile devices.

Evidence of sophisticated malware in the Pinduoduo app comes amid intense scrutiny of Chinese-developed apps like TikTok over concerns about data security.

Some American lawmakers are pushing for a national ban on the popular short-video app, whose CEO Shou Chew was grilled by Congress for five hours last week about its relations with the Chinese government.

The revelations are also likely to draw more attention to Pinduoduo’s international sister app, Temu, which is topping US download charts and fast expanding in other Western markets. Both are owned by Nasdaq-listed PDD, a multinational company with roots in China.

While Temu has not been implicated, Pinduoduo’s alleged actions risk casting a shadow over its sister app’s global expansion.

There is no evidence that Pinduoduo has handed data to the Chinese government. But as Beijing enjoys significant leverage over businesses under its jurisdiction, there are concerns from US lawmakers that any company operating in China could be forced to cooperate with a broad range of security activities.

The findings follow Google’s suspension of Pinduoduo from its Play Store in March, citing malware identified in versions of the app.

An ensuing report from Bloomberg said a Russian cybersecurity firm had also identified potential malware in the app.

Pinduoduo has previously rejected “the speculation and accusation that Pinduoduo app is malicious.”

CNN has contacted PDD multiple times over email and phone for comment, but has not received a response.

Pinduoduo, which boasts a user base that accounts for three quarters of China’s online population and a market value three times that of eBay (EBAY), wasn’t always an online shopping behemoth.

Founded in 2015 in Shanghai by Colin Huang, a former Google employee, the startup was fighting to establish itself in a market long dominated by e-commerce stalwarts Alibaba (BABA) and JD.com (JD).

It succeeded by offering steep discounts on friends-and-family group buying orders and focusing on lower-income rural areas.

Pinduoduo posted triple digit growth in monthly users until the end of 2018, the year it listed in New York. By the middle of 2020, though, the increase in monthly users had slowed to around 50% and would continue to decline, according to its earnings reports.

It was in 2020, according to a current Pinduoduo employee, that the company set up a team of about 100 engineers and product managers to dig for vulnerabilities in Android phones, develop ways to exploit them — and turn that into profit.

According to the source, who requested anonymity for fear of reprisals, the company only targeted users in rural areas and smaller towns initially, while avoiding users in megacities such as Beijing and Shanghai.

“The goal was to reduce the risk of being exposed,” they said.

By collecting expansive data on user activities, the company was able to create a comprehensive portrait of users’ habits, interests and preferences, according to the source.

This allowed it to improve its machine learning model to offer more personalized push notifications and ads, attracting users to open the app and place orders, they said.

The team was disbanded in early March, the source added, after questions about their activities came to light.

PDD didn’t reply to CNN’s repeated requests for comment on the team.

Approached by CNN, researchers from Tel Aviv-based cyber firm Check Point Research, Delaware-based app security startup Oversecured and Hyppönen’s WithSecure conducted independent analysis of the 6.49.0 version of the app, released on Chinese app stores in late February.

Google Play is not available in China, and Android users in the country download their apps from local stores. In March, when Google suspended Pinduoduo, it said it had found malware in off-Play versions of the app.

The researchers found code designed to achieve “privilege escalation”: a type of cyberattack that exploits a vulnerable operating system to gain a higher level of access to data than it’s supposed to have, according to experts.

“Our team has reverse engineered that code and we can confirm that it tries to escalate rights, tries to gain access to things normal apps wouldn’t be able to do on Android phones,” said Hyppönen.

The app was able to continue running in the background and prevent itself from being uninstalled, which allowed it to boost its monthly active user rates, Hyppönen said. It also had the ability to spy on competitors by tracking activity on other shopping apps and getting information from them, he added.

Check Point Research additionally identified ways in which the app was able to evade scrutiny.

The app deployed a method that allowed it to push updates without an app store review process meant to detect malicious applications, the researchers said.

They also identified in some plug-ins the intent to obscure potentially malicious components by hiding them under legitimate file names, such as Google’s.

“Such a technique is widely used by malware developers that inject malicious code into applications that have legitimate functionality,” they said.

In China, about three quarters of smartphone users are on the Android system. Apple (AAPL)’s iPhone has 25% market share, according to Daniel Ives of Wedbush Securities.

Sergey Toshin, the founder of Oversecured, said Pinduoduo’s malware specifically targeted different Android-based operating systems, including those used by Samsung, Huawei, Xiaomi and Oppo.

CNN has reached out to these companies for comment.

Toshin described Pinduoduo as “the most dangerous malware” ever found among mainstream apps.

“I’ve never seen anything like this before. It’s like, super expansive,” he said.

Most phone manufacturers globally customize the core Android software, the Android Open Source Project (AOSP), to add unique features and applications to their own devices.

Toshin found Pinduoduo to have exploited about 50 Android system vulnerabilities. Most of the exploits were tailor made for customized parts known as the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) code, which tends to be audited less often than AOSP and is therefore more prone to vulnerabilities, he said.

Pinduoduo also exploited a number of AOSP vulnerabilities, including one which was flagged by Toshin to Google in February 2022. Google fixed the bug this March, he said.

I’ve never seen anything like this before. It’s like, super expansive.

According to Toshin, the exploits allowed Pinduoduo access to users’ locations, contacts, calendars, notifications and photo albums without their consent. They were also able to change system settings and access users’ social network accounts and chats, he said.

Of the six teams CNN spoke to for this story, three did not conduct full examinations. But their primary reviews showed that Pinduoduo asked for a large number of permissions beyond the normal functions of a shopping app.

They included “potentially invasive permissions” such as “set wallpaper” and “download without notification,” said René Mayrhofer, head of the Institute of Networks and Security at the Johannes Kepler University Linz in Austria.

Suspicions about malware in Pinduoduo’s app were first raised in late February in a report by a Chinese cybersecurity firm called Dark Navy. Even though the analysis didn’t directly name the shopping giant, the report spread quickly among other researchers, who did name the company. Some of the analysts followed up with their own reports confirming the original findings.

Soon after, on March 5, Pinduoduo issued a new update of its app, version 6.50.0, which removed the exploits, according to two experts who CNN spoke to.

Two days after the update, Pinduoduo disbanded the team of engineers and product managers who had developed the exploits, according to the Pinduoduo source.

The next day, team members found themselves locked out of Pinduoduo’s bespoke workplace communication app, Knock, and lost access to files on the company’s internal network. Engineers also found their access to big data, data sheets and the log system revoked, the source said.

Most of the team were transferred to work at Temu. They were assigned to different departments at the subsidiary, with some working on marketing or developing push notifications, according to the source.

A core group of about 20 cybersecurity engineers who specialize in finding and exploiting vulnerabilities remain at Pinduoduo, they said.

Toshin of Oversecured, who looked into the update, said although the exploits were removed, the underlying code was still there and could be reactivated to carry out attacks.

Pinduoduo has been able to grow its user base against a backdrop of the Chinese government’s regulatory clampdown on Big Tech that began in late 2020.

That year, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology launched a sweeping crackdown on apps that illegally collect and use personal data.

The Personal Information Protection Law stipulates that no party should illegally collect, process or transmit personal information. They’re also banned from exploiting internet-related security vulnerabilities or engaging in actions that endanger cybersecurity.

Pinduoduo’s apparent malware would be a violation of those laws, tech policy experts say, and should have been detected by the regulator.

“This would be embarrassing for the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, because this is their job,” said Kendra Schaefer, a tech policy expert at Trivium China, a consultancy. “They’re supposed to check Pinduoduo, and the fact that they didn’t find (anything) is embarrassing for the regulator.”

Pinduoduo did not appear on any of the lists.

They’re supposed to check Pinduoduo, and the fact that they didn’t find (anything) is embarrassing for the regulator.

CNN has reached out to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and the Cyberspace Administration of China for comment.

On Chinese social media, some cybersecurity experts questioned why regulators haven’t taken any action.

“Probably none of our regulators can understand coding and programming, nor do they understand technology. You can’t even understand the malicious code when it’s shoved right in front of your face,” a cybersecurity expert with 1.8 million followers wrote last week in a viral post on Weibo, a Twitter-like platform.

CNN’s Kristie Lu Stout and Sean Lyngaas contributed reporting.

#152. Nvidia reinstates former CEO Jensen Huang despite China espionage scandal

Nvidia's board voted unanimously to bring back the disgraced CEO, who resigned this month amid news of his affairs. He's suspected of having had a relationship with a Chinese intelligence asset.

US tech company Nvidia said on Monday that it had reinstated Jensen Huang as its CEO "effective immediately."

This follows just a matter of days after his resignation after admitting to extramarital affairs, reportedly including a dalliance with a woman who was a Chinese intelligence asset.

The board unanimously decided that his return was in the "best interests of the company," Nvidia said, adding that it was satisfied that Huang had demonstrated his "candor and ability to lead."

Meanwhile, the 63-year-old said in a statement that he was "honored" to return to the company and that he would take on the renewed responsibility "with the greatest humility and renewed commitment."

He thanked interim CEO Colette Kress, who is set to return to her role as chief financial officer.

"I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support," Huang said. "Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can't wait to get back to work."

US President Donald Trump rapidly commented on the development online, saying it was the "correct and proper decision" and referring to Huang by his first name as a "Great Patriot and National Treasure."

"The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to Nvidia poses any risk to National Security," Trump wrote, also saying that the US had no evidence of him engaging in unlawful conduct.

Huang liked to flaunt his personal relationship with Trump. He was reportedly influential in convincing the US president to allow the export of higher-quality Nvidia chips to China that are useful in AI development than other US officials and entrepreneurs endorsed.

The decision was announced as trading started for the new week in New York.

The stock price of what investors deem the world's most valuable company has nosedived amid the scandal, with Nvidia's stock price falling from almost $220 (roughly €200) per share in late October to around $125 per share at the end of last week.

The announcement prompted a rapid early-morning rally on Wall Street, including Nvidia stocks rising back into a region between $160 and $170.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Huang quit earlier this month after admitting to extramarital affairs in a note to employees.

This concession came amid widespread reporting in the US linking him romantically to one woman in particular, who was running a major Nvidia client called Megaspeed based in Singapore and who was said to be an asset of Chinese intelligence services.

Her company is also suspected of diverting chips not approved for export to China to the Chinese market, circumventing US sanctions.

While these allegations have not been proven, they appeared to be based on the assessments of US and other western intelligency agencies, and to be information that was known for around a year. One possible indication of this was Singapore refusing the Chinese national entry into the country earlier in 2026.

#151. Dad who discovered daughter's murder on Facebook feels ignored by South African police

Okuhle's body was found dumped near a river in August. She had two children, aged three and nine, and was a civil engineering student

Tuku Nkosiyaphantsi found out his daughter had been killed from a post on Facebook.

It was August and he hadn't been able to reach 27-year-old Okuhle for days, although it wasn't unusual for her to drop out of contact from time to time.

Then one Saturday, two of Tuku's neighbours called him to say that they had seen that Okuhle had been reported missing by police on Facebook. They had also seen a photo of what appeared to be Okuhle injured.

"When I looked at this photo, I saw that the person in it was dead, and when I looked closer I realised it was Okuhle," says Tuku, 50.

After seeing the image, Tuku phoned a police officer he knew. The policeman confirmed the woman in the picture had been killed and her body dumped near a river in Kokstad, an agricultural hub in South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal province, in the east of the country.

But because the morgue was closed for the weekend, it wasn't until Monday morning that Tuku was able to identify Okuhle's body.

When he did, Tuku saw she had been mutilated and her face badly beaten.

"It was very painful, so much that I cannot accept it."

Okuhle's father, Tuku, says he feels "ignored and unseen" by the government after his daughter's death

Okuhle had two children, aged nine and three, and was a civil engineering student.

She is among 581 women who were killed in the country between July and September, according to the South African Police Service.

Overall, there were 5,590 murders - 204 fewer than in the same period last year.

It is unclear whether the number of women killed is an increase or decrease on previous years as police had stopped releasing this breakdown until now.

There has been a renewed national outcry this year about the scale of violence against women after the partially naked and bruised bodies of 12 women were found dumped in public areas in Ekurhuleni, a district to the east of Johannesburg, this summer.

South Africa has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence and femicide - the intentional killing of a woman or girl - in the world.

Am I Next? Fear and Survival in South Africa

The BBC World Service visits communities struggling to confrontÂ widespreadÂ violence against women

In response to this summer's killings, President Cyril Ramaphosa promised safety audits across every municipality to identify and address dangerous spaces for women, as well as an increased police presence in the worst-affected areas.

But in places like Kokstad, as well as Kempton Park, in Ekurhuleni, the BBC World Service saw people taking the protection of women into their own hands.

For Tuku, that means investigating his daughter's killing himself.

Months after she was killed, he says no-one has been arrested.

"It was just silent after we buried Okuhle - there was nothing at all. I so wish the police would stand up and investigate."

He believes police failed to review CCTV footage from a local government building in the town that may have shown who his daughter was with on the day she disappeared. The footage is wiped every seven days, he says.

The BBC approached the South African Police Service for comment but at the time of publication, no response had been received.

The police service has previously acknowledged shortcomings in its overall response to gender-based violence and femicide, adding that it was continuing to invest in addressing these challenges. Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia has said there needs to be "greater efforts" to prevent violence against women and children.

The killing of women this summer sparked widespread protests across South Africa

According to a 2024 report by the South African Medical Research Council, the number of unsolved cases of femicide was growing.

This year, Amnesty International said South Africa's police service was "under-resourced, poorly equipped, and insufficiently trained to respond effectively and sensitively to gender-based violence".

Tuku says he is now searching for CCTV footage and seeking out people who knew his daughter in the hope of finding leads.

Despite Ramaphosa's promises, he has little faith anything will change.

"I listened to Ramaphosa. The government acts only when something happened. We in Kokstad, we feel like we are ignored and unseen. The government does not care for us."

Asked earlier this month by the BBC what progress South Africa had made to keep women safe, Ramaphosa said the government would be allocating extra money in February's budget to deal with gender-based violence.

Speaking as he cast his vote in local elections, Ramaphosa added that the government had increased police numbers in the last three years "and we will continue to do so, so that there can be more visible policing".

Kokstad residents have started night-time patrols and are maintaining a curfew that advises children to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00

Okuhle is not the only woman to be killed this year in Kokstad.

Between January and October this year, the bodies of five women and three very young children were found in the town, with arrests only taking place in two of the cases.

In response, this summer, the community set up street patrols and a curfew for women and children.

Since June, children have been told to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00.

Kamvalethu Cetywayo, 34, from a local neighbourhood watch group, leads a group of around 15 men who patrol crime hotspots in the town at night, including areas where bodies have been found or trouble has been reported to them.

The patrols tend to take place between Thursday and Sunday because this is when people drink alcohol most heavily, says Kamvalethu.

Most of the patrollers carry sticks, whips and torches, but Kamvalethu has a licensed gun. He says the group will call police when they need back-up.

Asked how he feels about restricting the freedoms of women and children, Kamvalethu says the curfew helps keep them safe, is voluntary, and a temporary measure until police arrest the killers.

"With the resolution we made with the community, we get to assist them with this, but if people are refusing there's nothing we can do."

Even so, not all victims are attacked at night or on the streets.

Kgothatso says she was taking a taxi to work when the driver attempted to kidnap her

Kgothatso Mojela was kidnapped on her way to work in 2018 in Kempton Park.

She was in a taxi when the driver locked the doors and started driving in the wrong direction.

When Kgothatso told him he had missed the turn, she says he started punching and slapping her.

"Immediately, I just knew my life was in danger," says Kgothatso, who is now 35.

Kgothatso says she forced the passenger door open and threw herself out of the moving taxi, badly injuring her knee and causing nerve damage to her eyes. Two security guards, who were nearby, came to her aid.

She says her attacker was later jailed for a number of crimes, including what he did to her, but was released last year. Kgothatso says she now fears for her life.

Yet while Kgothatso was attacked by a stranger, according to the South African Medical Research Council, 60% of women murdered in the country between 2020-21 were killed by an intimate partner.

In the wake of her attack, Kgothatso has made changes to how she lives, including buying an imitation gun to scare off would-be attackers.

She has also stopped running alone, and insists on someone accompanying her if she goes to meet a client she hasn't met before at work.

Such precautions are all too familiar to many women in South Africa.

Zama says her running group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles

In September police urged women in the Kempton Park area to avoid walking or running alone, "particularly in isolated areas" - after the killing of 38-year-old mother Elizabeth Moselakgomo.

She vanished on 9 September while out running. Her badly bruised, partially clothed body was found dumped near a busy motorway in Kempton Park three days later.

It was a killing that resonated deeply within South Africa's running community, including sisters Zonke and Zama Mthethwa. They started The Pack, a women's running group in Johannesburg nine years ago. Elizabeth would sometimes attend The Pack events.

Grim discoveries of murdered women spark fear in South Africa

The South African men trying to end violence against women: 'Every man needs to play a part'

Runners across the city joined the search efforts following Elizabeth's disappearance, and took part in protests calling for violence against women to end.

Zonke and Zama's group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles. They also get cars to follow them and have started offering self-defence coaching to the women in their running group.

"We need to try and rally and create safe spaces for women to show up authentically and to do what they love doing," says Zama, 37.

Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at a prayer march to remember women who have been killed

Following her ordeal, Kgothatso moved from Kempton Park and now lives closer to her parents in another part of the country.

Her mother, a community activist, recently organised a prayer march to remember women who have been killed.

Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at the march.

Wiping away tears, she said: "To a survivor listening right now, I want to say you are not dirty, you are not broken beyond repair. You are not to blame and you are not alone."

This is part of the Global Women series from the BBC World Service, sharing untold and important stories from around the globe

#150. Anthropic shares fall below IPO price, a worrying sign for AI startups

Anthropic’s stock fell below its IPO price of $83, trading as low as $76 a share by midday Tuesday, down nearly 12% from Monday’s close.

Falling below the IPO price is often seen as a negative signal because underwriters typically price offerings at a discount to their expected trading value.

The AI industry has been eagerly watching how Anthropic’s shares trade, with VCs and other observers saying its performance could serve as a barometer for how public market investors value the sector.

The dramatic slump comes less than a week after Anthropic debuted on Nasdaq at $111.50 a share. If its shares continue to trade poorly in the coming weeks, the slide could put pressure on private startup valuations and weaken IPO prospects for other AI companies.

Anthropic isn’t the only AI stock selling off on Tuesday. Nvidia fell more than 7% by midday, giving back some of the more than 30%-plus gain it posted Monday after Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO.
